articles.title: Rouco, Lula pede para ministro do Meio Ambiente ler 2º discurso na COP31 | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente já tinha falado na cerimônia de abertura. Na segunda participação, no evento na Turquia, Lula passou palavra a João Paulo Capobianco, que leu mensagem preparada por ele.
articles.summary: Presidente já tinha falado na cerimônia de abertura. Na segunda participação, no evento na Turquia, Lula passou palavra a João Paulo Capobianco, que leu mensagem preparada por ele.
articles.body:
Com rouquidão, o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) pediu nesta quarta-feira (11) que o ministro do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, João Paulo Capobianco, lesse em seu lugar um dos discursos preparados para a COP31, em Antália, na Turquia.

🔎🌎 A COP31 é a 31ª conferência do clima da ONU, encontro anual que reúne representantes de diversos países para discutir ações de enfrentamento à crise climática. O Brasil sediou a COP30, em Belém (PA), em 2025.

O discurso na Cúpula de Líderes sobre Florestas seria o segundo do dia, depois de participar da cerimônia de abertura.

Ao passar a palavra ao ministro, Lula brincou com a situação e pediu que Capobianco o representasse de forma “efusiva”.

“Esse seria o discurso que eu ia fazer se eu tivesse bem garganta. Então, eu queria pedir, Capobianco, que você me representasse da forma mais efusiva possível. Não precisa falar rouco, não. Mas fale em tom de quem está fazendo muita coisa pela preservação ambiental", afirmou Lula.

Ministro do Meio Ambiente e Mudança do Clima, João Paulo Capobianco, na COP31. — Foto: Fernando Donasci/MMA

Na leitura do discurso, Capobianco abordou a proteção das florestas tropicais, o financiamento de políticas ambientais e o Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre (TFFF).

O texto preparado para Lula também afirma que a falta de recursos é um dos entraves para a proteção das florestas e defende uma maior participação de investimentos públicos e privados.

A mensagem cita ainda a redução do desmatamento no Brasil e afirma que o governo pretende transformar o chamado “arco da destruição” na Amazônia em um “arco da restauração”.

Presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva na COP31. — Foto: Fernando Donasci/MMA

"Vim a Antália com mandato renovado pelo povo brasileiro para aprofundar um projeto de governo que coloca o desenvolvimento sustentável no topo de suas prioridades.

Esta Cúpula de Líderes é especial porque coroa um processo inédito para os países detentores de florestas tropicais.

Nossa jornada começou em 2023, com a Cúpula da Organização do Tratado de Cooperação Amazônica.

Em parceria com a República do Congo, a República Democrática do Congo e a Indonésia, assinamos a Declaração “Unidos pelas Florestas”.

Na COP28, em Dubai, definimos o compromisso de deter e reverter o desmatamento e a degradação florestal até 2030.

Na COP30, em Belém, assumimos a tarefa de construir um Mapa do Caminho para alcançar esse objetivo.

A noção equivocada de incompatibilidade entre conservação e desenvolvimento pertence ao passado.

Estamos percorrendo um caminho que coloca os países detentores de florestas tropicais no centro das decisões globais sobre o clima.

Não mais como parte do problema, mas como protagonistas.

Reconhecer o valor da floresta em pé e dos povos que a preservam; pôr fim à devastação; e restaurar as áreas degradadas.

Temos diante de nós três desafios principais:

A degradação ambiental e o desmatamento estão relacionados a altos índices de violência e a baixos indicadores na área social.

A prosperidade baseada na floresta em pé também depende de políticas públicas que coloquem as pessoas como prioridade.

50 milhões de pessoas vivem no bioma amazônico sul-americano.

São habitantes de cidades de pequeno, médio e grande porte, que precisam de serviços, empregos e renda.

São comunidades ribeirinhas, indígenas, quilombolas que dependem diretamente da floresta e de suas riquezas.

São agricultores que sabem que é possível produzir sem aumentar as pressões sobre a vegetação nativa.

A bioeconomia é uma das alternativas à exploração predatória dos recursos naturais.

Sistemas alimentares que valorizam a agroecologia demonstram que é possível produzir alimentos, gerar renda, recuperar a natureza e fortalecer a resiliência às mudanças climáticas.

O turismo sustentável também pode valorizar as culturas locais e ampliar as oportunidades econômicas das comunidades.

Os saberes tradicionais devem ser associados à pesquisa científica e à tecnologia de ponta para gerar inovação e prosperidade.

O segundo entrave é a falta de recursos.

O mundo reconhece o valor das florestas, mas ainda não está disposto a financiar sua proteção na escala necessária.

Mobilizamos menos de um terço desse valor.

Em Belém, apresentamos ao mundo uma proposta inovadora, o Fundo Florestas Tropicais para Sempre.

A cooperação entre o Norte e o Sul Global é chave para proteger o planeta.

Esse mecanismo revoluciona a relação entre economia e conservação ambiental.

Não se trata de doação. Os investidores públicos e privados irão receber retornos financeiros sobre os recursos aplicados.

E os países que conservam suas florestas poderão contar com uma fonte constante de recursos para fortalecer suas políticas nacionais, respeitando suas próprias prioridades de desenvolvimento.

Com o TFFF, já mobilizamos 7,8 bilhões de dólares de diferentes parceiros internacionais.

A iniciativa conta com o endosso de 66 países e da União Europeia, incluindo países que concentram cerca de 90% das florestas tropicais do planeta.

A operacionalização do TFFF permitirá transformar compromissos em resultados concretos.

O terceiro obstáculo é a falta de liderança.

Em 2026, o enfrentamento da mudança do clima saiu da agenda do G7 e do G20.

O planeta não pode mais esperar enquanto guerras e conflitos comerciais consomem tempo e recursos escassos.

A falta de compromisso com a redução de emissões e descarbonização das economias é uma grave ameaça às florestas tropicais.

Se esses biomas ultrapassarem seu ponto de não retorno, o equilíbrio climático global pode se romper.

Quando existe determinação dos governantes, políticas públicas consistentes e participação da sociedade civil, aquilo que parece impossível começa a se tornar realidade.

A defesa e o desenvolvimento da Amazônia ocuparam um lugar central em meu terceiro mandato e continuará assim no quarto.

O Brasil combina prevenção, instrumentos econômicos, recuperação da vegetação nativa e bioeconomia para transformar a floresta em pé em fonte de renda e competitividade.

Nesta COP, apresentaremos nosso “Mapa do Caminho Nacional para interromper e reverter o desmatamento e a degradação florestal”.

Estamos no rumo certo para manter ou ampliar a área de vegetação nativa em nossos biomas até 2030, conforme nos comprometemos.

Registramos uma redução histórica no desmatamento em todos os biomas.

Na Amazônia, houve queda de 70%. No Cerrado, de quase 50%.

Acrescentamos 2,5 milhões de hectares de áreas protegidas ao patrimônio ambiental brasileiro.

Desde 2023, foram 20 terras indígenas homologadas - uma extensão territorial maior que a da Bélgica.

Essas ações, que vêm mudando a realidade na região, contaram com o inestimável apoio do Fundo Amazônia. O Fundo foi retomado e o número de parceiros foi ampliado.

Setenta e cinco por cento dos municípios amazônicos se beneficiaram de projetos do Fundo.

Estamos transformando o “Arco da Destruição” na Amazônia no “Arco da Restauração”, com dezenas de projetos de restauração florestal e sistemas agroflorestais.

Já recuperamos 4,5 milhões de hectares de solos e pastagens degradadas. A meta é chegar a 40 milhões em dez anos.

No próximo ano, inicia-se a Década das Nações Unidas para o Florestamento e o Reflorestamento, proclamada pela Assembleia Geral para o período de 2027 a 2036.

Nosso desafio será o de reunir vontade política, recursos financeiros e fomentar a cooperação internacional necessária para defender as florestas e as populações que vivem nesses biomas.

Essa é uma contribuição essencial para proteger o planeta dos efeitos nefastos da mudança do clima.

articles.title: Ministério da Justiça pede à PF esclarecimentos sobre afastamento de delegados | G1
articles.standfirst: Pasta enviou ofício à direção da PF sobre o afastamento dos delegados Daniel Cola e Wedson Cajé. Eles elaboraram relatórios sobre relação de ministros do STF com Vorcaro.
articles.summary: Pasta enviou ofício à direção da PF sobre o afastamento dos delegados Daniel Cola e Wedson Cajé. Eles elaboraram relatórios sobre relação de ministros do STF com Vorcaro.
articles.body:
O Ministério da Justiça informou nesta quarta-feira (11) que enviou um ofício à direção-geral da Polícia Federal em que pede esclarecimentos sobre o afastamento de dois delegados da coordenadoria-geral de repressão à corrupção, crimes financeiros e lavagem de dinheiro, Daniel Cola e Wedson Cajé.

O ofício foi encaminhado nesta terça-feira (10) em meio a uma crise na PF em razão dos desdobramentos das investigações sobre o caso Master.

Os delegados afastados de suas funções participaram da elaboração de relatórios sobre o envolvimento de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) com o ex-banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.

Os relatórios reuniam menções a três ministros da Corte: Alexandre de Moraes, Dias Toffoli e Kassio Nunes Marques.

A direção-geral da PF, comandada por Andrei Rodrigues, determinou que o material seja refeito. A cúpula da corporação afirma que o trabalho elaborado pelos delegados não seguiu orientações definidas pelo presidente do STF, ministro Edson Fachin.

Os novos relatórios deverão ser individualizados e abordar todos os ministros do STF que tenham sido citados, e não apenas Moraes, Nunes Marques e Toffoli. Segundo o blog do Valdo Cruz no g1 , há menções aos ministros André Mendonça, Luiz Fux e Gilmar Mendes.

Interlocutores ligados aos delegados afastados sustentam que a exclusão dos outros três ministros se deu porque não havia qualquer elemento suspeito contra eles.

Mendonça e Mendes, por exemplo, chegaram a votar contrariamente aos interesses do banqueiro em processos no STF.

O afastamento gerou reação da Associação Nacional dos Delegados de Polícia Federal (ADPF), que divulgou nota classificando o episódio como um "precedente grave" e apontando risco de retaliação e ameaça à autonomia dos investigadores.

Em meio à escalada da crise, o diretor-geral Andrei Rodrigues pediu o desligamento da entidade após 24 anos filiado.

Em resposta às críticas, a Polícia Federal afirmou que mudanças de chefia são atos estritamente discricionários de gestão de pessoal, pautados por "conveniência e oportunidade administrativa".

A instituição destacou ainda que a substituição nas chefias não desfalca nem altera os delegados e equipes que presidem os inquéritos em andamento, como os das operações Compliance Zero, sobre as fraudes do Master, e Sem Desconto, que apura desvios no INSS.

A resposta da PF ao pedido de esclarecimentos do Ministério da Justiça deve conter essas informações.

Andrei Rodrigues, diretor-geral do PF, em CPI no Senado — Foto: Andressa Anholete/Agência Senado

articles.title: STJ investiga patrimônio de ex-servidor preso por vazamento | G1
articles.standfirst: Em entrevista ao GloboNews Radar, presidente do STJ, Luis Felipe Salomão, afirmou que apuração é sigilosa. Humberto Pradera teria vazado dados a advogado amigo de Flávio.
articles.summary: O ministro Luis Felipe Salomão confirmou que o STJ apura a evolução patrimonial de Humberto Pradera, preso por repassar informações ao advogado Willer Tomaz.
articles.body:
O presidente do Superior Tribunal de Justiça (STJ), Luis Felipe Salomão, afirmou que o tribunal está aprofundando as apurações internas sobre o patrimônio do ex-chefe da Tecnologia do tribunal Humberto Pradera.

Em entrevista ao GloboNews Radar , Salomão disse que a investigação corre em sigilo mas que o patrimônio dele é tema de aprofundamento em apuração interna.

“Aprofundamos a investigação, sobre a questão patrimonial do servidor, sobre os procedimentos que ele adota e adotou para poder investigarmos, para sabermos a extensão dessa questão”, disse Salomão.

“Estamos avançando sim com o procedimento que já foi feito na Polícia Federal . Esse inquérito começou no Rio Grande do Sul com apuração sobre desvio e lavagem de dinheiro sobre bets. Apreendeu-se o celular do advogado [Willer Tomaz] , obteve-se conversa do advogado e uma delas envolvia o ex-servidor do STJ", completou o presidente da Corte.

Segundo Salomão, a partir da identificação da conversa do advogado com o servidor, a notícia chegou ao STJ, que compartilhou provas e adotou medidas com relação à conduta do ex-chefe da TI. "Ele foi desligado, as senhas dele foram cortadas", declarou Salomão.

Na entrevista à GloboNews , o ministro também detalhou as medidas tomadas para evitar novos vazamentos.

“A providência também permitiu que nós adotássemos programas internos para reforçar a segurança digital, identificar acesso, permitir controle maior. Só pode acessar as decisões, essas minutas, quem tem procedimentos mais específicos. Estamos adotando uma série de providências para poder manter essa segurança digital mais acentuada agora”, explicou.

O STJ aprofunda sua apuração interna a partir da investigação que já corre na PF sobre Willer e Flávio Bolsonaro.

Segundo a investigação, Pradera teria facilitado o acesso indevido do advogado Willer Tomaz a informações de processos em tramitação no STJ.

Willer Tomaz é amigo do ex-candidato à Presidência, senador Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ). Willer e Flávio são investigados em um inquérito no STF sobre suposta lavagem de dinheiro.

Humberto Fontoura Pradera, ex-servidor do STJ suspeito de vazar informações sigilosas — Foto: Redes sociais/Reprodução

articles.title: Crise na PF pode adiar investigação de ministros do STF para 2027 | G1
articles.summary: A crise na PF, agravada pelo afastamento de delegados no caso Banco Master, deve atrasar o envio de relatórios ao STF sobre as citações ao banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro.
articles.body:
A crise na Polícia Federal em meio às investigações sobre o escândalo do Banco Master pode cair como uma luva para uma ala do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ).

Isso porque a divisão na PF vai acabar levando a um adiamento para o ano que vem da análise pelo tribunal sobre o envolvimento de ministros com o banqueiro Daniel Vorcaro, atrasando a decisão sobre quem será, ou não, investigado dentro do Supremo. Há um risco de que tudo fique para 2027.

Uma ala do STF, aliada ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes , busca retardar ao máximo uma decisão sobre o que fazer com os magistrados que foram citados em mensagens retiradas do celular de Daniel Vorcaro.

A estratégia é tentar um acordo e fazer com que ninguém seja investigado pelas relações com o banqueiro, evitando com isso dar mais munição para bolsonaristas tentarem aprovar um impeachment de ministros do Supremo no próximo ano.

A crise na PF se acentuou depois que o diretor-geral do órgão, Andrei Rodrigues, afastou dois delegados que fizeram relatórios iniciais sobre como três ministros – Alexandre de Moraes, Nunes Marques e Dias Toffoli – aparecem nas mensagens do celular de Daniel Vorcaro.

Além disso, Andrei determinou que os relatórios fossem refeitos. A Associação dos Delegados da Polícia Federal (ADPF) criticou a decisão do diretor-geral, que se desfiliou da entidade, aumentando a tensão dentro do órgão .

Há uma guerra de versões sobre o afastamento dos delegados e o pedido para que os relatórios sejam refeitos. A cúpula da PF diz que os relatórios foram elaborados de forma incorreta.

Os delegados que comandam a ADPF dizem que o motivo seria outro, que o conteúdo dos documentos não agradou a direção da PF . A crise está instalada e tende a adiar tudo dentro da instituição.

Agora, os relatórios terão de conter os nomes dos seis ministros mencionados no celular do banqueiro. Além de Moraes, Nunes Marques e Toffoli, aparecem também nas mensagens Gilmar Mendes , André Mendonça e Luiz Fux .

Os delegados que deixaram seus postos na investigação do caso Master alegaram que, contra esses ministros, não há nada comprometedor . Pelo contrário. Os dois primeiros até votaram contra os interesses do banqueiro no STF.

Segundo a cúpula da PF, a orientação desde o início era que os seis magistrados constassem do relatório que será encaminhado ao presidente do STF, Edson Fachin .

A promessa é que o documento seja enviado ainda em novembro. Só que o prazo vai ficando curto para ser analisado neste ano, já que o STF entra em recesso na segunda metade de dezembro.

Diretor-geral da PF, Andrei Passos Rodrigues, é ouvido na CPI do Crime Organizado — Foto: Andressa Anholete/Agência Senado

articles.title: JOHN YOO: The blue tsunami’s real target is the independence of the Supreme Court
articles.summary: Donald Trump's midterm landslide loss threatens the Supreme Court as leading Democrats push court-packing plans from nine to 13 justices now.
articles.body: The 2026 midterms' astounding election results not only shift control of Congress but also portend two years of hostility with President Donald Trump. The blue tsunami also threatens the independence of the Supreme Court. As Democrats exercise their newfound power in the legislature and build on their majorities in years to come, they will try to interfere with the workings of basic American institutions. Of these promised "reforms," expanding the Supreme Court may pose the greatest threat to the American system of limited government and natural rights. The Democrats’ landslide victory is hard to overstate. As many political observers predicted for a midterm election during a president’s second term, Democrats took control of the House from the governing party. But few foresaw the force of the rejection of President Trump and the Republican Party. With 24 races still to be called, Democrats have won 254 seats, surpassing the 218 needed for a majority, with Republicans left with only 157. The results in the Senate were perhaps even more shocking. Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats, giving them a 54-44 majority; Democratic challengers narrowly lead the Republican incumbents in the other two races. What was equally amazing was that Democratic victories came in Republican strongholds, such as Kansas (where a Democrat had not won in a century), Texas, Iowa, South Carolina and Ohio. TRUMP'S SUPREME COURT MAJORITY FACES LOOMING THREAT AFTER DEM SENATE TAKEOVER: 'STUCK' Conservatives are panicking that the shift in control of the Senate will threaten their majority on the Supreme Court. Presidents George H.W. Bush and George W. Bush appointed three of the justices (Chief Justice John Roberts and Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito), while President Trump appointed three more (Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett). Presidents Obama and Biden, meanwhile, appointed three (Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson). This 6-3 majority, unified generally by an originalist approach to constitutional interpretation, has delivered some of the highest priorities on the conservative wish list: the overruling of Roe v. Wade and the return of the abortion question to the states; the declaration of the Second Amendment’s individual right to possess firearms; and the end of racial preferences in government programs and university admissions. The change in Senate control in January means that no conservative justice is likely to retire until 2028. UNDER-THE-RADAR IMPLICATION OF DEM BLUE WAVE MEANS 'ZERO' CHANCE GOP ACCOMPLISHES CRITICAL GOAL, EXPERTS WARN The problem, simply put, is time. Thomas is 78, while Alito is 76. For justices appointed since 1980, the average age at retirement or death in office is 79.8 years. If Thomas or Alito were to leave office over the next two years, which would be in keeping with that average, the Democratic majority would be unlikely to confirm their successors. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., has already set a precedent of not filling a Supreme Court vacancy in the last year of a presidential term — he did not allow a Senate vote to fill the 2016 vacancy created by Justice Antonin Scalia’s death. It would be a small political jump — though a serious change in Senate norms — for Democrats to extend that period to two years. The change in Senate control in January means that no conservative justice is likely to retire until 2028. In the interest of full disclosure, I served as a law clerk to Justice Thomas in 1994-95, and I do not want him to ever retire. Indeed, I would be shocked if he left office while he could physically perform the duties of the office. DEMOCRATIC SENATOR CLAIMS GOP 'STOLE' TWO SCOTUS SEATS IN 2016, 2020, CALLS FOR EXPANSION The political changes launched by the midterm elections could make matters worse for conservatives. The betting odds are that Democrats will win the 2028 presidential election. An incumbent party usually loses at the end of its president’s second term in office. Putting aside the unique control of the Virginia dynasty from President Thomas Jefferson through James Monroe, a two-term presidency has only been succeeded by a president of the same party twice: Martin Van Buren and George H.W. Bush. Both examples reflected the popularity and success of the departing incumbents, Andrew Jackson and Ronald Reagan. If anything, last week’s tallies reveal Trump’s deep unpopularity. It would require an unprecedented election to beat this historical pattern and return a Republican to the presidency in 2028. And even if Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio were to win, they would likely still face a Democratic Senate, which would narrow, if not completely eliminate, their ability to appoint a committed originalist to the Supreme Court. The prospect of Democratic control of the Senate and possibly the presidency for the next six years has prompted short-term maneuvering to install a young originalist on the Court during the lame-duck congressional session over the next few weeks. Justice Alito, however, has publicly declared he will not retire this year, and, as I have said, I would be shocked if Justice Thomas were to even entertain the idea. The idea that President Trump could persuade either justice to retire in favor of a younger replacement is more characteristic of inside-the-Beltway politicking than of serious long-term political thinking. If the Democrats were to build on their majorities and win the presidential election in 2028, we may well see not just different faces on the bench — we may see an entirely different kind of Court altogether. Almost every leading Democrat demands "reform" of the Supreme Court by expanding its size from nine to 13 or more justices. Several members of the House and Senate, such as Rep. Jerry Nadler and Sen. Adam Schiff, have introduced bills to add more justices. Leading presidential candidates, such as former Vice President Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., have blessed the idea of court-packing. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., expressed the feelings of left-wing Democrats well: "We need to expand this morally bankrupt court from nine to 13." Expect House and Senate majorities to send court-packing bills to the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office for signature. While President Trump will surely veto them, as he should, the Democratic Congress will not pass the bills in the hope they will become law in the next two years. Instead, they will force House and Senate members to take public votes on court-packing in preparation for the real show, which will take the stage when a Democrat wins the White House in 2028. Once progressives have a governing trifecta, court-packing legislation will sail through both houses again and meet with the approval of a Democratic president. The Supreme Court will become the political plaything, not just of Democrats, but of both parties, which will surely add more seats to the Court whenever they control both elected branches of government. That will do more in the long run to destroy the independence of the federal judiciary, on which our natural rights against the tyranny of the majority rest, than any short-term maneuvering over justices and their retirement dates. articles.title: Did Democrats save Pete Hegseth from impeachment?
articles.summary: Eleven Democrats are absent from procedural vote that narrowly shelves House impeachment vote against defence secretary.
articles.body:
The United States House ⁠of Representatives has blocked an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a surprise reprieve for President Donald Trump’s administration as Republicans reel from their midterm election defeat .

The impeachment articles were introduced by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie, but the effort was backed primarily by Democrats. They accuse Hegseth of abuses of power and conducting illegal military operations.

The Republican-led House voted 211-204 on Tuesday to refer the articles back to the House Judiciary Committee, where they could remain indefinitely. The procedural move in effect killed the impeachment drive for the duration of the current Congress’s term, which ends in eight weeks. On January 3, Democrats will take control of the House and Senate.

In a twist, the absence of 11 Democratic lawmakers during the vote proved decisive.

Here’s what to know about the vote to block Hegseth’s impeachment and what could happen next:

The vote was not on whether to impeach Hegseth. It was on whether to refer the articles of impeachment to the Judiciary Committee, where they may be further investigated or amended.

Such procedural moves are often used as stalling tactics. With the current Congress due to conclude soon, the resolution is unlikely to return to the House floor before its term ends.

Massie called the vote “a procedural motion to kill the resolution”.

Massie was the sole Republican to oppose the measure. The remaining votes fell along party lines with Republicans supporting the measure and Democrats opposing it.

Eighteen representatives were absent from the vote – 11 Democrats and seven Republicans. Had the Democrats shown up and voted with their colleagues, they would have had the numbers to defeat the procedural move, forcing a full House vote on whether to impeach Hegseth as early as this week.

Trump cheered the result of Tuesday’s vote in a social media post, saying the Democrats’ impeachment effort had “miserably FAILED!”

Who were the 11 absent Democrats, and why did they miss the vote?

The Democrats absent from the vote were:

The representatives have given varying explanations for why they did not show up.

Strickland, Jackson, Stansbury and Gillen all blamed a traffic delay in Washington, DC.

Pelosi said she was in her home state for a veterans event while Correa said he was in California before undergoing a health procedure. Horsford’s office cited a personal emergency.

Pettersen, who said she helped introduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth in April, said she had been “denied the ability to vote on this motion” without elaborating.

Jackson, Stansbury, Gillen, Strickland, Horsford, Pelosi and Pettersen all said they would have joined their Democratic colleagues in opposing the measure. Jackson and Stansbury also said they had formally recorded their opposition in the Congressional Record although this does not change the official vote count.

There was no immediate comment from Stevens, Brownley or Wilson on their absences.

Stevens previously criticised the Trump administration for launching the war on Iran with Israel and sought more congressional oversight. But days before the US midterm elections on November 3, the Michigan congresswoman, who had lost the Democratic primary for the state’s open Senate seat earlier to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers against her own party’s nominee.

Wilson, 83, on Monday attended the groundbreaking for a housing project in Miami-Dade County. Wilson and Brownley, like Stevens, previously opposed Trump’s handling of the war on Iran and demanded the administration seek congressional approval for the fighting.

Democratic politicians and progressive commentators have expressed outrage that poor attendance from Democrats impacted the outcome of the vote.

Congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove from California said: “We knew that this vote was coming, so people should have gotten their raggedy selves up these steps to vote.”

“There is no reason why we should have lost this vote because of attendance issues,” she added.

Senator-elect El-Sayed, responding to a question about the absent Democrats, said: “You should show up and do your job.”

Some pundits pointed the finger at Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the new speaker of the House in January. They accused him of failing to exert sufficient pressure on party members to defeat the measure.

Political commentator Krystal Ball called the vote “a major Hakeem Jeffries fail”.

Only eight officials – all federal judges – have ever been convicted by the Senate. Trump has been impeached twice – in December ⁠2019 and January 2021 – but the Senate acquitted him on both occasions.

articles.title: Trump's judicial confirmations to face resistance in Democratic-controlled Senate
articles.summary: A Democratic-controlled Senate is unlikely to help President Trump and Republicans continue their push to remake the federal judiciary in the next two years.
articles.body:
Washington — After seeing success in reshaping the federal judiciary in his first term and the initial two years of his second administration, President Trump and Republicans' campaign to shift the courts to the right could be coming to an end with Democrats poised to take control of the Senate next year.

During his first term in office, Mr. Trump successfully put more than 230 judges on the federal bench, including three justices on the Supreme Court, remaking the judicial branch for decades. So far during his second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 of the president's judicial picks. In total, Trump nominees make up about one-third of active federal judges .

But Democrats are now poised to control at least 54 Senate seats , and as many as 56 depending on the outcome of races in Mississippi and Alaska, making it unlikely that Mr. Trump will fill many more vacancies on the U.S. district and appeals courts.

"No one, or nearly no one, is going to get confirmed, so what he does in terms of nominating people, we'll see," Ed Whelan, a distinguished senior fellow at the Ethics and Public Policy Center and former law clerk to the late Justice Antonin Scalia, told CBS News.

There are currently 28 vacancies on the federal courts and another 15 seats that will open up in the coming weeks and months. So far, the president has formally sent to the Senate 16 nominees for those existing and future vacancies, though it's possible he submits more names for consideration before the current Congress finishes its work. Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social earlier Tuesday three more nominees to district courts in Texas and South Carolina.

The GOP-led Senate Judiciary Committee is moving quickly to advance those picks before control of the upper chamber changes hands. It voted to advance four of the president's district court candidates and held confirmation hearings for four other judicial nominees Tuesday.

The panel is expected to hold more confirmation hearings next week, a break from committee practice of holding those proceedings every other week, according to a source familiar with the panel's workings.

Republicans are violating "numerous longstanding standards in a desperate attempt to confirm more than 30 qualified loyalists to lifetime appointments before Democrats take the majority," Sen. Dick Durbin, the top Democrat on the Judiciary Committee, said Tuesday.

Durbin raised concerns about two of Mr. Trump's latest picks to serve as federal judges in Texas: James Sullivan, who lost his bid for reelection to the Texas Supreme Court last week, and T. Elliot Gaiser, the head of the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel whose only tie to Texas is a one-year clerkship for a judge on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit.

The Judiciary panel received information from Sullivan after he lost his campaign for Texas Supreme Court justice last week and from Gaiser on Nov. 8, before the president announced his intent to nominate each man, according to the source. Both are slated to appear before senators for confirmation hearings next week.

"There are many things we still can do, and I hope we'll use them. And one of them is not to expedite nominees who have not been carefully vetted," Durbin said. "I hope we don't accept that as a standard in this committee."

But Sen. Chuck Grassley, an Iowa Republican who chairs the Judiciary Committee, pushed back on Durbin's claim that he is departing from its typical practices. He argued that there are no committee rules about how quickly it can move to hold confirmation hearings or when those proceedings are held, and said chairs have discretion to set the panel's schedule.

"Historically, this committee has shortened timelines when circumstances warrant it," he said.

In anticipation of Democratic control of the upper chamber, Republicans are expected to make judicial nominees a focus of the lame-duck period.

"The priority is going to be getting the judges across the finish line," Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters Monday.

But seats on the federal bench that remain open come the end of the current Congress are likely to remain unfilled for at least the next two years.

"For the past two years, we've seen Trump seeking to stack our courts — district courts, circuit courts — with loyalists to him and not to the Constitution, and I think he's going to try to continue to do that," Rachel Rossi, president of the Alliance for Justice, a progressive judicial advocacy group, said. "In this moment, when Trump has clearly created this litmus test that there must be loyalty to him and not the Constitution, it's hard to see how Democrats can support nominees going forward."

It is not unprecedented in the Senate for the party in control to stymie the nominations of a president in the opposing party. During the final two years of former President Barack Obama's administration, when Republicans held the Senate majority, just 20 of his nominees to the district and appeals courts were confirmed. Obama's final judicial confirmation came six months before the end of his second term. Among the candidates that did not get a vote from the GOP-led Senate was Merrick Garland, who was nominated to replace Scalia on the Supreme Court following his death in February 2016.

"What we've seen is the federal courts being stacked with extremists and loyalists, and now Democrats have the power to stop the reshaping of our courts in a very dangerous direction," Rossi said. "I think there's increasing visibility on what judges mean and what these lifetime seats mean, and the hope is that Democrats use their power and stand against any further reshaping of our judiciary."

Of the 43 current and future vacancies, Mr. Trump has not yet announced candidates for more than half of those seats. Many of those are in states that will be represented by either two Democratic senators or one Republican and one Democratic senator next year.

Democrats could work with the White House to find consensus on candidates to serve on the district courts in their states, but it's unclear whether there is an appetite from either side to do so.

"Republicans on the Senate Judiciary Committee and the Trump administration have gutted the committee's oversight and confirmation authority," Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, a Rhode Island Democrat who is expected to lead the panel next year, said in a statement. "There needs to be accountability for years of Republican bad behavior, and a hard reset on the nominations process next Congress."

Democrats' rout of Republicans in last week's midterm elections also makes it unlikely a Supreme Court justice appointed by a GOP president steps down in the final two years of Mr. Trump's term, given that a successor would likely not clear the Senate.

The president made a significant impact on the nation's highest court, appointing three of the nine justices. Among those was Justice Amy Coney Barrett, who filled Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg's seat following her death in September 2020, during Mr. Trump's first term.

Justices Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76, are the two oldest members of the high court, but Alito told The Wall Street Journal in August, "I'm here for another term." Alito also told CBS News chief legal correspondent Jan Crawford last month that while he considered retirement earlier this year, he feels he can still make a contribution to the Supreme Court.

With neither justice expected to step down during the lame-duck session, it could be several years before there is both a GOP president and Senate in place to confirm their potential successors on the Supreme Court, raising concerns among conservatives that a Democratic president and Senate could fill the seats of the influential conservative justices.

"Trump has managed to put in jeopardy his biggest achievement," Whelan said.

articles.title: Jordan looks to move Republicans beyond midterm rout
articles.summary: House Republicans on Tuesday tapped Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) to lead their diminished conference in the next Congress, betting that a conservative spitfire —...
articles.body:
House Republicans on Tuesday tapped Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) to lead their diminished conference in the next Congress, betting that a conservative spitfire — and onetime leadership nemesis — can restore the fight to a party battered by the midterms and scrambling for a path back to power.

In brief comments right out of the gate, Jordan set the tenor of the coming clash, vowing to fight the ascendant Democrats on the size and scope of federal power — an issue that's taken on fresh significance with the arrival of a new crop of democratic socialist members.

"When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom," Jordan told reporters in the Capitol shortly after his victory at a press conference where new leaders declined to take questions. "And we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day."

Jordan's task is not only to bring together the warring factions of a restive party demoralized by their election rout and sniping over who's to blame but also to craft a message that will resonate with alienated voters ahead of the 2028 elections — all while defending President Trump from the myriad investigations the Democrats are promising into the president's family, allies and administration.

It was the size of the election losses, some Republicans said, that tipped the scales toward Jordan over Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the outgoing majority leader whose many years in the leadership ranks became a liability, rather than an asset, after the midterm landslide.

"He represents change," said Rep. Darin LaHood (R-Ill.). "He also has a very detailed plan on how we get out of the minority. He has excellent communication skills. He's viewed as a fighter, which he is, and I think the conference was ready for a different direction."

"If the election would have been closer last week," he added, "I think the results could have been different today."

For Jordan, the ascension represents an extraordinary arc for a right-wing renegade who built a brand in the Capitol for taking on party leaders, not joining their ranks.

The Ohio Republican is a co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, a bloc of iconoclastic conservatives who have routinely butted heads with GOP leadership over government spending and, at times, blocked Republican legislation in an effort to yank the party further to the right. He is also chair of the House Judiciary Committee, a role he's used to launch investigations into Democrats and other Trump political opponents.

"Jim Jordan is a fighter. I think he doesn't mind saying the hard things, but he's level-headed, and he's going to be able to work with a lot of different personalities to stay focused on the mission and get the job done," Rep. Sheri Biggs (R-S.C.) said.

If Tuesday's leadership elections were a referendum on the midterm results, however, they also didn't supply the "clean slate" some GOP lawmakers were hoping for.

Rep. Tom Emmer (Minn.), the Republican whip, fended off a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger (R-Texas) to keep his post. And Rep. Lisa McClain (Mich.), the GOP conference chair, will also remain in place after beating back challenges from Republican Reps. Greg Steube (Fla.) and Erin Houchin (Ind.).

"This Republican leadership team will expose the Democrats' lies and show the American people their true colors as the radical communists that they are," Emmer said after his win.

Trump stayed out of the leadership races — an unusual move for a president who has exerted his influence in past contests. Many Republicans are blaming Trump's policies — particularly the Iran war, global tariffs and a deportation surge — for dragging down GOP candidates in the midterms. Some even suggested they chose Jordan because he expressed a willingness to break from the president on certain issues.

Rep. Rich McCormick (R-Ga.) said he asked Jordan what the Republican conference was going to do "now that we have to deal with a president who we're not sure … how he's going to go forward."

"I thought he gave a very good answer, which was instead of waiting to see what the president's going to say, we lead. We lead with a message based on what we want to say, and that's what I've always tried to do myself. I mean, each individual has to know their individual district as well as possible," McCormick said.

"We're independent thinkers, right? … I want to not worry about what the president says. I want to have my own opinion, and … what's funny is the president usually comes around to what I believe anyway. And if he doesn't, that's OK because we're not a cult. If everybody in the church agrees with everything the minister says, you're in a cult. We are not a cult. It's very high time to realize that. And it goes back to the Reagan rule, right? It's OK if you disagree with me on a certain percentage. We can still be on the same team," he added.

The leadership transition, from Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to Jordan, could not offer a more stark contrast in styles and personas.

Johnson is a constitutional lawyer, prim and bespectacled, who often quotes Bible verses and borrowed church terminology in pledging to be a "servant leader." Jordan is a former champion wrestler, still fit and muscular, who's known for eschewing a blazer around the Capitol and jousting routinely with Democrats from his perch atop the Judiciary Committee.

The House Freedom Caucus repeatedly tried to tap Jordan to run against former Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.), which he resisted. But after McCarthy was ousted, it spurred a contentious 2023 battle for the Speakership between Scalise and Jordan.

Scalise initially won the Republican nomination for Speaker then, defeating Jordan in a secret-ballot vote. But, he later withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support to secure the gavel. Jordan was later chosen as the nominee for Speaker, but he repeatedly fell short of the votes needed to clinch the post.

"It's almost like this is the right time for him," Rep. Tom Cole (Okla.), a member of the House Republican Steering Committee and the top Republican on the House Appropriations Committee, told reporters after the vote.

"I think we need, you know, a combat guy, so to speak. But he's as good at political combat as anybody I've ever seen. So I think he'll do an excellent job for us."

Rep. Nicole Malliotakis (R-N.Y.) also said she sees Jordan as a unifier despite his staunch conservatism.

"Jim Jordan is somebody who's a fighter, somebody who's thoughtful when he speaks," she said. "He's eloquent. He doesn't miss a beat. He's out there talking about the issues, talking about what people are thinking. I think he'll do a good job. Look, I'm one of the more centrist members. … He brings everybody together."

"I think the reason I had supported him for Speaker two years ago, I thought he was the one who could bring everybody together because he had relationships with more moderate members, with the Freedom Caucus folks, and everybody in between," she added. "So I think you know he handles himself in a way that he can get the job done."

Congressional Democrats were quick to criticize the pick as another instance of the GOP conference committing itself to a far-right pick after an election that they view as a resounding rejection of Trump.

"Stephen Miller and Jim Jordan," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.) wrote on social media, noting the promotion of Trump's White House adviser to chief of staff.

"Republicans learned absolutely nothing from what happened a week ago, and are responding by elevating their most extreme voices to positions of power."

"I think you look at our conference, we're a significantly more conservative conference than what we were coming into this," Rep. Brian Mast (R-Fla.) said, referencing the number of moderate members who lost their reelection bids.

"And I think if you look at that, you're going to see us push our conservative values."

Rep. Michael Cloud (R-Texas), a member of the House Freedom Caucus, asserted voters still wanted Trump's agenda and said he also saw Jordan as a figure who could fight any eventual impeachment effort that Democrats might bring against Trump.

"He's a conservative. He's also a smart strategist. He's definitely a good communicator, and especially where we're headed with the Dems, who seem obsessed with impeachment and, you know, shenanigans, he's had to lead the defense on that before," Cloud said.

"So I think we'll be well prepared headed into the future."

articles.title: Small-town Marine veteran refuses to back down in 16-year fight for America's forgotten heroes — and wins
articles.summary: Scott Stump, a Marine veteran from North Carolina, spent 16 years battling Congress and bureaucracy to build the Desert Storm memorial on the Mall.
articles.body: A Marine veteran from a small North Carolina town spent 16 years fighting to build a national memorial honoring the Americans who served in Desert Shield and Desert Storm — overcoming congressional setbacks, years of bureaucratic hurdles and a lengthy battle over its location, all while refusing to use taxpayer money to get it done. "I'm just an average everyday American," Scott Stump told Fox News Digital. "I just felt like something had to be done to correct what I felt was a historical oversight." What began as one veteran's determination to ensure the sacrifices of the 1990-1991 Gulf War generation were not forgotten became a 16-year undertaking that culminated in the Oct. 24, 2026, opening of the Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial on the National Mall. Stump, who spearheaded the effort with a team of veteran volunteers, said he insisted from the beginning that the project be built without U.S. taxpayer funding, even as it required years of congressional action, federal approvals and financial support from donors. TRUMP SIGNS ACT CLEARING THE WAY FOR MEDAL OF HONOR MONUMENT ON NATIONAL MALL "I made the decision right off the bat that [I] was not interested in encumbering the taxpayer at all," Stump said. "This should be 100% privately funded. Just felt like it was the right thing to do." Stump said the idea first came to him in November 2010, as the country approached the 20th anniversary of Operation Desert Storm, the U.S.-led military campaign that liberated Kuwait from Iraqi occupation. He had attended veterans events where service members from other conflicts were recognized, but those who fought in Desert Shield and Desert Storm were overlooked. SIX AMERICAN HEROES EVERYONE SHOULD KNOW THIS MEMORIAL DAY, FROM DELTA FORCE TO A WWII BOMBER CREW "They skipped right over it, and they act like it never happened," Stump recalled. Living in Waynesville, North Carolina, Stump had no elaborate political operation or established Washington network to carry out his vision. Instead, he assembled a team of fellow veterans who shared his belief that the conflict deserved a permanent place in the nation's history, he said. Stump worked with then-Rep. Phil Roe, R-Tenn., and Sen. John Boozman, R-Ark., to secure the legislation necessary to authorize the memorial. "It was kind of a ‘Mr. Smith Goes to Washington,’" Stump said, referring to the classic film about an ordinary American navigating Washington politics. EXCAVATION SET TO BEGIN ON TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S 250-FOOT TRIUMPHAL ARCH AMID LEGAL BATTLE The legislative effort alone took roughly three and a half to four years, and Stump said he was forced to start over after legislation introduced late in one congressional session failed to advance. He reintroduced the effort in 2013, testified before Congress in February 2014 and watched the House approve the measure in a unanimous 370-0 vote on May 28, 2014. Stump said the Senate effort encountered additional legislative complications that threatened to derail the memorial authorization before the congressional session ended. He fought to clear the obstacle, knowing another failure could mean starting the legislative process from scratch for a third time. The authorization ultimately passed as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for fiscal year 2015, which President Barack Obama signed into law in December 2014. LAWYER SAYS 250-FOOT TRUMP ARCH DISRUPTS HISTORIC SIGHTLINES CHERISHED BY VETERANS SEEKING BURIAL AT ARLINGTON Next came the challenge of securing a location worthy of the service members the memorial would honor. Stump initially believed the site-selection process would take approximately 18 months. Instead, it stretched to 39 months, he recounted. He said much of that time was spent educating officials and members of federal commissions about the significance of Desert Shield and Desert Storm. Some questioned whether the conflict had truly ended, he said. Others questioned whether enough Americans had died to justify a prominent national memorial. "’There weren't enough people who died to have a memorial for this,’" Stump recalled being told during the approval process. After initially receiving approval for a different location, Stump and his team continued pushing for their preferred site near 23rd Street and Constitution Avenue. FEDERAL JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS CONSTRUCTION OF TRUMP'S ARLINGTON TRIUMPHAL ARCH HOURS AFTER APPROVAL They secured approval on June 21, 2018, in an "absolute epic battle," Stump said. "We are not interested in just something visible," Stump said, recalling the argument he made to commissioners. "But we wanted something that was visitable." He wanted visitors to do more than pass a monument on their way to another destination. He wanted them to walk through the memorial, experience its design and leave inspired to learn about a war that had faded from the memories of many Americans. Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, prompting President George H.W. Bush to launch Operation Desert Shield and build an international coalition. After months of military buildup, Operation Desert Storm began Jan. 17, 1991, with weeks of airstrikes before a ground offensive launched Feb. 24 drove Iraqi forces from Kuwait in approximately 100 hours. GOLDEN EAGLES, LIONS AND A WINGED LADY LIBERTY TOP TRUMP'S PROPOSED 250-FOOT DC TRIUMPHAL ARCH DESIGNS "You know, you have 30 some odd countries, five continents, different races, religions, creeds," Stump said. "It's a wonderful story." Outside of the monument this month, DJ of Wisconsin told Fox News Digital his mother served in the Air Force as a nurse in the early '90s. She was never deployed overseas, but during her time, she worked with many veterans from Desert Storm. "[The memorial] reminded me of her and her service, and just the thanks that I have both for her and for all Americans who sign a blank check for the country that can be paid for up to and including their lives. So, I'm just very thankful, and this is a good, good, humble reminder of that sacrifice," said DJ. Desert Storm veteran Steve from Indiana told Fox News Digital he was "impressed" that the memorial was so close to the Lincoln Memorial and the Vietnam Memorial. "In some ways, Desert Storm is somewhat forgotten. It was a relatively small war, but a very successful one, and I think there are a lot of lessons to be learned from that war," said Steve. DAKOTA MEYER TALKS SERVICE, BLASTS CONTROVERSIAL DESIGN FOR GLOBAL WAR ON TERROR MEMORIAL The Department of the Interior and National Park Service formally welcomed the Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial to the National Mall in Washington, D.C., in October, honoring the Americans who served. "The Desert Shield and Desert Storm Memorial honors the courage of the Americans who answered our nation’s call, the sacrifice of those who never returned home and the families who supported them," Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said. Stump said he intentionally structured the organization behind the memorial as an association rather than a traditional foundation, allowing the project to maintain a singular focus on completing the monument rather than supporting a permanent payroll or other long-term institutional expenses. He added he did not want future operating costs to force compromises in the design. "Our job, and I believe that we've achieved it through a wonderful design, a wonderful design team that worked extremely hard to come up with what we have, is to make an emotional connection with the visitor," Stump said. He pointed to the Korean War Veterans Memorial as an example of how a monument can move visitors even when they know little about the conflict it commemorates. Young people, he said, often encounter the memorial's statues of soldiers wearing ponchos and leave wanting to understand the war behind those figures. articles.title: Dakota Meyer survived a battle he thought would kill him. 15 years after leaving the Marines, he went back
articles.summary: Dakota Meyer reenlisted in 2025 and completed reconnaissance Marine training at 38, calling it the hardest thing he's ever done in his life.
articles.body: Fifteen years after Dakota Meyer left the Marine Corps, the Medal of Honor recipient decided to put the uniform back on — becoming the first with the award to ever reenlist. Meyer was 36. He had fought in Afghanistan, struggled with the transition home from war and spent years building a life outside the military. But he said the desire to serve never went away. "Every day after I took that uniform off, that desire to serve didn't just end because my commitment to the country did," Meyer told Fox News Digital in an interview ahead of Veterans Day. AMERICAN WAR HERO DETAILS DIRE LIVING CONDITIONS US TROOPS FACE AS HEGSETH TAPS HIM TO 'FIX' IT Meyer rejects the idea that receiving the Medal of Honor meant he had already done enough. "I think sometimes it's looked at as you've done your part, and I am wholeheartedly against that," he said. "I believe that the only time you've done your part is when you've done all that you can." For Meyer, Veterans Day is a reminder that service does not necessarily end when someone leaves the military. "Sometimes we look at the veteran title as it is something that represents something we've done," Meyer said. "And it's not. It's something that we are doing, and it is something that we can continue to do." Meyer reenlisted in 2025 and later entered the training pipeline to become a reconnaissance Marine, completing the grueling course in his late 30s. "To be able to do that at 38, it was definitely one of the — hands down — probably the hardest thing that I've ever had to do," Meyer said. His first stint in the Marines had taken him to Afghanistan, where at 21 he fought in the 2009 Battle of Ganjgal in Kunar Province. Meyer had been assigned to remain with the vehicles at a rally point while other members of his team accompanied Afghan troops toward the village roughly a mile away. The patrol was ambushed by more than 50 insurgents firing from fortified positions on the surrounding slopes. MEDAL OF HONOR RECIPIENT JAMES CAPERS JR. SAYS RECOGNITION IS BITTERSWEET AFTER LOSING 'SO MUCH' Meyer and Staff Sgt. Juan Rodriguez-Chavez could hear the battle unfolding over the radio. Four members of Meyer's team were trapped inside the ambush. After repeatedly asking for permission to go in, Meyer and Rodriguez-Chavez drove toward the fighting, with Meyer manning the gun turret. "I think often we try to make these decisions as if it's some heroic decision, and it's really not," Meyer said. "It's just about following through on what my promise that I had made to them." The pair made repeated trips into the ambush, helping evacuate wounded troops as Meyer continued searching for his teammates. "I think it was at that point that I did realize that I just accepted that I was going to die," Meyer recalled. "But I was gonna make sure that I would do everything I could up until that last breath." His four teammates were ultimately found dead. Meyer would receive the Medal of Honor for his actions that day. Leaving the Marines the following year brought a different battle. "I struggled. I mean, I struggled," Meyer said. "The horrors of war definitely haunted me when I got out." Meyer said one of the hardest parts of returning to civilian life was figuring out what could replace the sense of purpose he had found in the military. "The hardest part was finding purpose," he said. "It wasn't about being successful in anything." Eventually, he said, he realized that neither money nor professional success was what he was looking for. He wanted to feel that his work had an impact. Years later, while speaking to a group of Marines at Camp Pendleton, that question of purpose came back to him in a different way. A Marine attending a leadership course told Meyer he was deciding whether to reenlist. He had a family and could make more money outside the military, but he loved serving. "Do you think it's still worth serving?" he asked. Meyer said yes, but the answer bothered him. "I felt it was one of the most unbecoming things that I had ever said back to that crowd," Meyer said, explaining that he was telling someone else to accept the sacrifices of continued service while he was free to return to civilian life. "I told them that I would walk out of there and I would go about reenlisting, or I would never say that to anybody again." It ultimately took Meyer about two years to return to the Marines. Once back, he pursued a goal he had held since first seeing a Recon Marine poster in a recruiting office as a young man. "They were the people that we were all trying to be inside of the Marine Corps," Meyer said. At 37 and 38, keeping up physically wasn't necessarily the problem, but recovering felt different. "What got me was the cumulative fatigue at my age," Meyer said. "These kids can recover like nothing else." The experience also gave Meyer a close look at a generation of Marines nearly two decades younger than the one he had served alongside in Afghanistan. He came away impressed. "When we talk about service members or this next generation being weaker, it's absolutely not the case," Meyer said. "These kids are hands down, they will rise to the level of expectation that is set for them." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Meyer said the Marine Corps itself has changed since he left in 2010, but he viewed much of that change as necessary. He recalled younger Marines giving him an hour-long lesson on their "new language" during a break in training and said he often found himself learning from them. "They do things a lot smarter," Meyer said. "I found myself learning a lot more from them than I did them probably learning from me." He said today's young service members don't have a "generational problem," and said they still want the challenge, purpose and sense of belonging that drew those to serve before them.

articles.title: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt objects at Biden outside Irish university
articles.summary: Three men have been arrested after protesters pelted objects at  former President Joe Biden during protests outside a university in Dublin, police in Ireland said.
articles.body: Three men have been arrested after protesters pelted objects at former President Joe Biden outside a university in Dublin, police in Ireland said Wednesday. Videos showed protesters, some waving Palestinian flags, chanting “Blood on your hands” and scuffling with police officers outside Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday, as he attended a ceremony honoring his son Hunter Biden, alongside former first lady Jill Biden. White liquid, believed to be milk, could also be seen flying through the air toward the group. Hunter Biden was being honored by its traditional Hist debating society, which dates back to 1770. Previous recipients of the gold medal for outstanding contribution to public discourse include Irish musician Bob Geldof, South African Bishop Desmond Tutu, WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange and the late Sen. Ted Kennedy. During his acceptance speech, Hunter Biden discussed his addictions, family life and being in the public eye. “We are living in an age of bullies,” he said, adding that he had learned this from “my own scars.” Shortly after the ceremony, a “protest took place in Trinity’s Front Square,” Catherine O’Mahony, a spokesperson for the college, said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday. She said “the protest escalated while the Bidens were leaving,” and Irish police, known as the Gardaí, arrived at the scene. “The Biden family left without incident. The protest dispersed soon after,” she added. Police said in a statement Wednesday that three adult males were arrested “in relation to a public order incident” at Trinity College Dublin. One man in his 50s “has since been charged and is due to appear before Court. The two other males have been released without charge.” The statement did not say what the man had been charged with. Representatives for the elder Biden did not immediately reply to a request for comment about the incident. Ireland has long had a historical solidarity with the Palestinian cause, with pro-Palestinian flags, murals and graffiti a common sight around the country. Many in the country compare the current situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank with Ireland’s experience of British colonial rule and struggle for self-determination. Ireland was also the recent venue for American rapper Macklemore’s sold-out “Free Palestine Tour,” which opened in Dublin last month. The Bidens, who have Irish heritage, also met with Ireland’s Taoiseach, or prime minister, Micheál Martin. “We reflected on his strong Irish roots and previous visits, appreciating his lifelong support for Ireland,” Martin said in a post on X, of his meeting with the former president. During a 2023 visit to the country while he was president, Biden told the Irish parliament in an emotional address that he was “home.” Biden’s great-great-grandfather Owen Finnegan left the Irish county of Louth for the United States in 1849, and he also has relatives from another side of his family in County Mayo, on Ireland’s west coast. Earlier this week, Biden, 83, signaled he was scaling back public tours to promote his upcoming memoir “Promise Me, America,” as he continues his treatment for cancer. “Some days are better than others,” Biden wrote Sunday in a lengthy post on X. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.” Biden announced that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer months after he left office in January 2025 and has since undertaken courses of radiation therapy and hormone treatment. He said his doctors were “encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment” and thanked the public for their prayers and well-wishes.
