articles.title: Senate Republicans plan 54-day blitz to push Trump's agenda before Democrats seize power
articles.summary: John Thune and Senate Republicans agreed to a resolution to maximize their remaining 54 days in power before Democrats take control next year.
articles.body: With their leadership elections settled, Senate Republicans are gearing up to "maximize" their remaining time in power before Senate Democrats take over next year. All eyes are again on Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., who was re-elected to another term as the Republican leader. Shortly after winning, Thune declared that he and the Senate GOP were "committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can." "That means extending the calendar here, the number of days we're here, the number of hours we're here, the number of votes we may end up taking," Thune said. "But we are going to finish this legislative session strong." SENATE GOP REBELLION FIZZLES AS THUNE KEEPS POWER DESPITE HISTORIC MIDTERM MASSACRE The Senate was initially set to be in roughly 20 days from Tuesday until the changing of the guard, but Republicans are now squeezing the juice out of every last minute to ram through must-pass legislation, dozens of President Donald Trump’s nominees and more. And Republicans agreed to hold themselves to that sprint until the end of the year at the tail end of their marathon closed-door meeting on Tuesday. Lawmakers plan to "maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3," according to a resolution agreed to in the meeting obtained by Fox News Digital. Another crack at budget reconciliation could be the trickiest part of their ambitious year-end gauntlet, particularly depending on what lawmakers try to cram into the process. GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS "I think we've got to keep it realistic to probably have any chance of passing, pretty narrow," Thune told Fox News Digital. Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who chairs the Senate Budget Committee responsible for developing the scaffolding around the process, told Fox News Digital that he intended to present his plan to Republicans during their lunchtime meeting on Wednesday. It’s also where Republicans are considering one last attempt at getting the SAVE America Act, or a version of it that could pass muster with the Senate rules referee. "Oh yeah, that'd be part of it, you know, to provide funding for states for election integrity type of measures," Johnson said. Defense funding will be another major task for Republicans, given that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and Democrats are determined to use Congress’ power over the nation’s purse strings as a way to choke off spending on the Iran war. SENATE REPUBLICAN PUSHES OVERHAUL TO CUT RED TAPE AND SPEED UP AMERICAN ENERGY PROJECTS Thune acknowledged that reconciliation could be another landing spot for Pentagon dollars to flow, but hoped Democrats would choose a different route. "It's going to depend on whether or not they have any of their members who are persuaded that making sure that we have enough munitions and ammo and weaponry to be able to defend the country is a priority," Thune said. "I hope they do, in which case maybe we won't have to go down that path, but we're scoping it out right now." One of the White House’s top priorities, and at the top of Thune’s to-do list, is confirming a slate of judicial and executive branch nominees. As of Tuesday, there were 23 judicial nominees, many of whom still needed to go through committee, and nearly 100 executive branch nominees that need confirmation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There is a slew of other high-priority items that were punted to the lame duck, like the National Defense Authorization Act, a bipartisan permitting reform package and keeping the government funded. Preventing another shutdown, or at least hammering out a deal, could be tricky given how the political winds shifted after the election. Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., who serves on the Senate Appropriations Committee, told Fox News Digital that "where we can clear the decks, the better," to fund the government. "I know that prior to the election that was the thought of some of our Democratic colleagues as well, but we have to be able to work together to get some of that done," Britt said.

articles.title: Betrayal after service: Let’s do better for our veterans
articles.summary: Veteran advocates dub it “institutional betrayal” when the institutions charged with caring for veterans leave them feeling dismissed or abandoned.
articles.body:
“We will not rest until all of America’s great veterans can receive the care they so richly deserve,” President Trump said — a sentiment echoed by presidents of both parties going back decades.

But for many veterans who come home seeking help with chronic pain, blast-wave brain injury, PTSD, depression, toxic burn pit exposure or moral injury, the reality can be a maze of bureaucratic indifference resulting in delayed or disjointed care.

Veteran advocates dub it “institutional betrayal,” a term describing a rupture of trust when the institutions charged with caring for veterans leave them feeling dismissed or abandoned.

It’s not hard to see why institutional betrayal is an issue for vets and their advocates, given the size of the health care system veterans must navigate. The sprawling Veterans Health Administration, which is part of the Department of Veterans Affairs, operates the largest health system in the U.S., providing care to more than 6 million veterans, many of whom are dealing with complicated health issues associated with military service as well as typical ailments.

The consequences can be debilitating and dangerous. When veterans meet obstacle after obstacle in their search for diagnosis and treatment, they may begin to withdraw and disconnect from support networks.

Withdrawal and subsequent isolation are especially concerning. Isolation is a well-known precursor to suicide. And suicide, at rates far above civilians, remains a tragic consequence for U.S. veterans — especially younger veterans, for whom it is one of the main causes of death.

Just how prevalent isolation is among veterans is highlighted in the data. In a 2025 suicide report, the VA found that about 61 percent of veterans who died by suicide in 2023 were not receiving VA care in the year before their deaths. That alone suggests a system that too often fails veterans before crisis becomes visible.

Despite efforts over the years by Congress and successive administrations of both parties to address problems in the sprawling Department of Veterans Affairs and in the hand off of military personnel to the VA, the evidence is powerful of lingering dysfunction that pushes veterans away and instils a sense of betrayal that only reinforces the isolation.

In 2025, the Government Accountability Office reported that VA still had not fully implemented key recommendations for the community care program, including establishing standard time frames for when care appointments must occur after referral. The program is a critical element in veteran care, allowing vets to receive wellness services from non-VA providers when VA facilities are too distant or cannot provide timely care.

The same agency’s separate 2025 report concluded that, although the situation is improving, the VA still relies on several different scheduling systems. The complexity creates challenges for schedulers and veterans, contributing to delays in care.

“Because of concerns with wait times and other issues … VHA health care continues to be on our high-risk list,” the agency found.

The VA’s Office of Inspector General reached similar conclusions in recent reviews. In a 2024 snapshot of the Martinsburg VA Medical Center in West Virginia, inspectors found a backlog of more than 5,000 active community care consults — requests to receive care from in-network providers outside of VA medical facilities.

They also found that the medical facility was taking longer than 45 days on average to make veterans an appointment for community care — the requirement is that this take no longer than seven days. Some vets were waiting 100 days or longer for VA staff to contact them after requesting a medical consult or referral.

At the VA center in Boston , the inspector general also noted a lethargic bureaucracy with delays in setting appointments for veterans for more than half of direct and community care referrals.

The problems are systemic. As noted by the non-profit Concerned Veterans for America , since 2020 “the VA’s Office of Inspector General has issued over 50 reports highlighting the significant deficiencies the VA system has and why is it unable to provide consistent, timely, high-quality care to veterans.”

The system’s dysfunction and the sense of institutional betrayal are compounded by the military services’ inability to ensure personnel are treated effectively before they leave the armed forces.

For example, the Government Accountability Office last year found that in a review of records of 50,000 servicemembers leaving the military, two-thirds worried they might have mental health problems requiring a clinical follow-up, yet more than half refused referrals. The findings suggest that treatment is lacking while in the services and that personnel are not sufficiently encouraged to seek help.

That failure of military leadership is troubling because the year immediately following uniformed service can be fraught with both physical and mental health issues.

In a study of veterans , VA researchers found that at both three and nine months after leaving the military, 53 percent of respondents said they had chronic physical health conditions, while nearly 33 percent reported chronic mental health conditions at both time intervals, including depression.

That is a significant concern because suicide is major problem in those first months following separation — in fact, a RAND study found that the risk of suicide steadily increases during the first year after separation.

U.S. veterans, says the Veterans of Foreign Wars in a statement, “are forced to navigate a bureaucratic labyrinth that too often grinds them down, delays their care and treats them with suspicion from day one.”

Frank Larkin is a former Navy SEAL who served as the 40th U.S. Senate Sergeant at Arms. He is also the father of a Navy SEAL son who died by suicide and chairman of Warrior Call, a national nonprofit aimed at curtailing suicide among veterans and service members.

articles.title: FIRST ON FOX: Supreme Court justices confront what it will take to keep America's founding freedoms alive
articles.summary: Supreme Court justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett urged Americans to study civics education as the nation turns 250.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: As America celebrates 250 years of independence this year, three conservative Supreme Court justices are warning that preserving the nation's founding freedoms for future generations depends on Americans understanding their history, embracing civic education and actively participating in their system of government. Justices Brett Kavanaugh, Neil Gorsuch and Amy Coney Barrett each implored Americans to familiarize themselves with their system of government and the history behind it to ensure that the nation’s legacy is preserved. Though the three conservative justices were united in their call for civic education, they each approached the topic differently in a series of interviews filmed by the Federalist Society and obtained by Fox News Digital. The videos come ahead of the Federalist Society's 2026 National Lawyers Convention this week, which spotlights "250 Years of American Exceptionalism." Gorsuch, for instance, struck a distinctly religious tone. GORSUCH HIGHLIGHTS STAGGERING DECLINE IN CIVIC LITERACY THAT PROMPTED HIM TO AUTHOR NEW BOOK "I think it's very easy to take the rights granted in our Constitution and the ideals expressed in the Declaration for granted," he said. "They are, for us, a little bit like the air we breathe and the water a fish might swim in. They seem natural to us, but they weren't in 1776. The ideas in the Declaration of Independence that all of us are created equal, that every one of us has God-given rights — they don't come from government, they come from God." Gorsuch, who was appointed to the court by President Donald Trump in 2017 following the death of Justice Antonin Scalia, went on to describe the importance of historical study to the preservation of the American way of life. THE UNWINNABLE WAR AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS FOUGHT AND WON CHANGED HUMAN HISTORY FOREVER "Our country is a blessing from God, and that we owe great thanks for it, and we have great responsibility for it," he went on. "The reason why our Constitution and Declaration have survived is because people choose it anew in every generation. You need to know its history. You need to know what you're preserving. Daniel Webster said it took 6,000 years for us to generate a system of government like this. Don't expect that to happen easily or again." Kavanaugh, similarly, emphasized the importance of education. "I think our education system is absolutely fundamental to ensuring that in the next 250 years, we preserve this republic and improve upon this republic. So, teaching American history, teaching the values of this country, the history of this country, why this country exists, how this country has been preserved, how this country has been improved over time, for example, by our constitutional amendment process and otherwise," the justice, appointed to the bench following a tumultuous confirmation process in 2018, said. "And I think all of us should be constantly striving to ensure civics education, not only for our youth, but for all of us, and that we constantly are learning and participating in our system of government," he continued. SPEAKER JOHNSON WARNS STUDENTS ARE 'INDOCTRINATED' TO SEE US THROUGH 'WRONG LENSES' AS NATION CELEBRATES 250TH The Federalist Society filmed its interviews ahead of its National Lawyers Convention, which will bring together minds from across the conservative legal movement to discuss matters deemed pressing. While not interviewed by the Federalist Society, Justice Sonia Sotomayor shared her thoughts on America's 250th anniversary during an event at Mount Vernon's Washington Library, taking a slightly darker tone than her conservative colleagues. During her talk, which centered primarily on civic engagement, Sotomayor argued that the United States is in a rough place at the moment and that it would take "some hard work" for it to get back on an "even keel." "There are some norms we may have lost forever," she said. "But I don’t think that we will fail as a democracy. But I think we’re going to have a hard patch figuring out what that means." Barrett, meanwhile, focused on the Declaration of Independence and how she believes it should inspire civic participation today. "We're not passive observers in the American project. We're participants in it. It is our project," she said. "I might suggest that people look at the last line of the Declaration of Independence. It ends with a mutual pledge in which the signatories to the document mutually pledge their lives, their fortunes and their sacred honor to the success of the American project. And they made good on that promise. Some lost their fortune, lost their property to loyalists ... and they pledged with their honor not to deviate from the commitments that they had made in signing the Declaration of Independence." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Surely that's the kind of commitment that it takes to have it keep going forward," said Barrett.

articles.title: Read the studies: Rage over data centers is mostly the product of ignorance
articles.summary: Perhaps Hollywood trained us too well to fear Skynet, when in fact the real trouble is in the wires.
articles.body:
Seven in 10 Americans oppose an AI data center in their community, whereas only 53 percent would object to a nuclear power plant, according to Gallup’s March survey . Somehow, we would rather live beside a reactor than a building full of servers.

Perhaps Hollywood trained us too well to fear Skynet, when in fact the real trouble is in the wires.

To be sure, there have been instances where data centers were simply built in inappropriate places, too close to unwilling neighbors. But most of the fear rests on a belief that data centers are the reason your electrical bill keeps climbing. But the best evidence through 2024 says they explain only a small slice of it. The panic is steering us away from the technology and away from the fixes that would protect your wallet. Ignorance has a price here, and it is showing up on your monthly statement.

Candidates in both parties ran against data centers. Texas Democrat James Talarico said , “Data centers are jacking up utility bills across the state of Texas.” His Republican opponent, Attorney General Ken Paxton, answered with a four-point plan of his own . New York also froze permits for new large data centers for up to a year .

Talarico has a fair point about the bills. Residential prices in his state’s market rose by roughly 30 percent from 2021 to 2025 , and Gov. Greg Abbott told regulators to make data centers pay for the infrastructure they need. But blaming one kind of building for all of them is the mistake.

I have been a California ratepayer since 1990. My own bill has climbed every year, despite the solar panels I installed on my roof. I don’t live near a data center. So rather than just get angry at my power bills and rail against data centers, I decided to read the studies first and try to understand, at this early date in the AI era, what has happened so far.

A Wharton and Harvard Business School working paper attributes just 4 percent of residential rate increases from 2020 to 2025 to new data centers. MIT researchers put the residential effect at just 2.1 percent for 2010 through 2024.

An EPRI working paper found that, through 2024, a doubling of a state’s data center capacity was actually associated with a 3.5 percent drop in residential electricity prices. That makes sense — when there are more users to cover the same fixed grid costs, everyone’s share is less. But the arithmetic cuts both ways — EPRI’s researcher cautioned that prices could rise if utilities build for demand that never shows up.

So what is causing bills to go up? Adjusted for inflation, the national average price in 2024 matched 2019. So the pain is concentrated in specific places for specific reasons.

Berkeley Lab’s review of 2019 through 2024 points to unglamorous culprits. Inflation-adjusted distribution spending rose 35 percent. California’s big three utilities were authorized to recover $27 billion in wildfire costs, which grew from 1.7 percent of their revenue requirement in 2019 to 17 percent by mid-2024. California’s residential prices rose nearly 40 percent over that stretch, amid only modest data center growth . Pay no attention to the man behind the curtain who ignored common-sense timber and brush management.

PJM Interconnection, the nation’s largest regional transmission organization, estimates that data center load added $23.1 billion in costs across the last three capacity auctions . Of the $6.5 billion tied to data centers in December’s auction, about $6.2 billion traced to facilities not yet built . Customers are paying for buildings that exist only in a utility forecast. That’s a risk allocation failure, and I’ve seen enough of those in private credit to recognize one.

The fix is old-fashioned contract discipline. Ohio regulators now require large new data centers to pay for at least 85 percent of subscribed capacity for up to 12 years , with collateral behind the promise . The old tariff’s minimum billing floor was 65 percent . Virginia’s new large-customer class, starting January 1, 2027, demands 14-year commitments and minimum payments on 85 percent of transmission and distribution demand and 60 percent of generation. Wisconsin regulators required the largest data centers to fund 100 percent of the generation resources built to serve them.

In private credit, we call that “take-or-pay.” The customer who asks for the plant carries the risk of the plant. Washington’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, signed March 4 by seven tech companies , points the same way, but it is voluntary . A pledge becomes protection only when a utility commission writes it into a tariff.

The other half of this equation is supply. PJM Interconnection’s market monitor counts a 6,520 megawatt gap in the 2027-2028 auction and wants a separate capacity auction for data center load , open only to new generation. We can also permit generation and transmission faster.

Nuclear belongs in the mix, on a 2030s clock: Google’s deal with Kairos Power targets 500 megawatts by 2035 , and the Energy Department is cost-sharing up to $800 million for reactors under construction for the Tennessee Valley Authority and Holtec Government Services, with completion expected in the early 2030s.

Blanket moratoria, meanwhile, may forfeit the cost-spreading effect researchers found through 2024. They do nothing about the supply gap.

Diogenes Laertius recorded Socrates as holding that there is only one evil — that is, ignorance . And Aung San Suu Kyi put it this way: “It is not power that corrupts but fear.” So don’t just get mad about data centers. Ask your commission whether there is a large-load tariff, what is being built in your area, and who is carrying the risk. Fear the stranded cost, but welcome the technology.

Jay Rogers is President of Alpha Strategies and a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.

House Republicans came together Tuesday to shelve a measure to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , thanks largely to almost a dozen Democrats failing to show up for the early evening vote.

Some of the Democrats who did cast a vote did not even try to hide their frustration.

“The people send us here to do a job. I don’t know if anyone had any real health issues or anything significant. So I want to leave room for that,” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio Cortez (D-N.Y.) told CNN’s Manu Raju . “But that being said, at the end of the day, we’re here to do a job. And the same way I had to clock in when I worked at a restaurant, we got to clock in and do our work here.”

Some of the members missed the vote, which ended around 6 p.m. EST, due to gridlock on Pennsylvania Ave., caused by a traffic accident.

“Like other Members of Congress, Rep. Stansbury was blocked from entering the Capitol to vote due a traffic incident and a police escort of a bus during the vote,” Rep. Melanie Stansbury ‘s (D-N.M.) office said in a statement on the social platform X. “When she reached the chamber, the vote had just gaveled out.”

“The Congresswoman was stuck behind a motorcade and missed the vote by 1 minute. She would have voted against the motion to refer,” Rep. Marilyn Strickland ‘s (D-Wash.) chief of staff said .

The House voted to refer the resolution to committee, allowing Republicans to stop it from advancing during the lame-duck session. The 211-204 vote effectively punted any efforts to impeach the Pentagon chief until Democrats take back the majority.

The 11 Democrats who missed the vote were Stansbury, Strickland and Reps. Julia Brownley (Calif.) Lou Correa (Calif.), Laura Gillen (N.Y.), Steven Horsford (Nev.), Jonathan Jackson (Ill.), Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), Brittany Pettersen (Colo.), Haley Stevens (Mich.) and Frederica Wilson (Fla.).

Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.), who introduced the impeachment articles, was the only Republican to oppose the move to impede his measure.

Democratic leaders supported Massie’s resolution but said they did not pressure rank-and-file members to do the same, calling it a vote of conscience for each member.

Rep. Pete Aguilar (Calif.), the chair of the House Democratic Caucus, said they “didn’t put our fingers on the scale,” and played down the idea that Democrats would race to try and impeach Hegseth again in the next Congress.

“When we are in the majority, we are serious about holding people accountable, and that will … start early with oversight,” Aguilar said. “But that is not anything that is being discussed at this point.”

Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to take the Speaker’s gavel next term, predicted Hegseth would be gone soon.

“If he was an honorable individual, which he’s not … he should have just stepped down. As opposed to putting the country through this type of proceeding, when it’s all unnecessary, given the fact that we know at the end of the day that Pete Hegseth is not going to be around for much longer.” Jeffries told Spectrum News NY1 in an interview.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) made a similar prediction on his podcast earlier this week.

“And one of two things is going to happen: either Hegseth is going to step down, either he will resign voluntarily or Trump will fire him. Or, if that does not happen, I think it is extremely likely, if not certain, that the House will impeach him,” Cruz said Monday on an episode of “The Verdict.”

“Because, on the face of it, the votes are there. Now, it only takes a majority to impeach,” he added.

Ahead of the evening vote, Hegseth held his first press conference at the Pentagon in more than six months and strongly pushed back against Massie’s impeachment effort, dismissing the Kentucky Republican as“one disgruntled and defeated congressman” who is following “a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.”

The president celebrated the vote in a social media post Tuesday night.

“Victories in Venezuela and Iran, the Best Recruitment Numbers in the History of the Military (Long waiting lists to get in!), and Spirit like rarely seen before, led to the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot,” President Trump wrote last night after the vote.

“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America,” Trump continued. “They must be stopped!”

MINORITY REPORT: Sen. John Thune (S.D.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (Ohio) will hold the minority leader positions in the incoming Congress after prevailing in caucus elections on Tuesday.

Thune was reelected to be the GOP’s Senate leader after a daylong battle and delays in votes Tuesday.

The Republican conference meeting Tuesday was only supposed to last a few hours but turned into an all-day event after Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) and other conservatives pressured Thune to commit to bring a budget reconciliation package to the Senate floor during the lame-duck session.

“I appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest conversation with my colleagues today, and I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress,” Thune wrote in a statement.

Jordan was voted to be the new House minority leader for the Republican Party in a 106-73 vote over Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.).

Jordan has spent nearly two decades in the House and is a co-founder of the House Freedom Caucus — the most conservative bloc in the House.

Minnesota Rep. Tom Emmer (R) will be the next minority whip , defeating fellow GOP Rep. August Pfluger (Texas) for the position. Emmer had served as the No. 3 Republican in the majority.

TIME’S UP? : Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) said during a press conference Tuesday afternoon that they would not back Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) to hold the Senate majority leader position.

Schumer, the current Senate minority leader, has received opposition from both progressive and centrist Democrats.

“We need leadership that’s going to govern for the entirety of the caucus, for folks from blue states, purple states and red states,” Slotkin said Tuesday.

Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen (Md.) has been floated as a possible candidate to challenge Schumer for the position but has made it known that he is only in “listening mode” at this time. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), among a handful of new faces who committed during their campaigns to oppose Schumer, said he’d support Van Hollen.

Schumer told reporters on Tuesday he’s confident he’ll ultimately win. Democratic Sens. Ruben Gallego (Ariz.) and Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.) noted at a separate press conference that they will continue to back the New York lawmaker.

“It’s time for us to unify, we are going to work together as a caucus and put a plan together about how to move forward for what the country wants us to do, and I think, you know, we have the person who’s going to lead us there,” Gallego said.

ALASKA GAP WIDENS: Former Rep Mary Peltola (D) expanded her lead over Sen. Dan Sullivan after the latest batch of ballots was counted in Alaska overnight.

Peltola’s lead increased from 2,517 to 4,250 votes. Significantly, that also puts her total ahead of the combined vote share for Sullivan and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a former schoolteacher that her campaign allegedly recruited into the race. The other Sullivan now has 4,027 votes.

The consumer price index (CPI) report released yesterday showed prices rose 0.4 percent on a monthly basis in October, higher than the 0.3 percent that economists polled by FactSet predicted.

Economists at the Congressional Joint Economic Committee, as well as at The New York Times, calculated an annual inflation rate of roughly 4 percent in October. The previous month, the official annual inflation rate was 3.7 percent.

Federal Reserve board of governors member Christopher Waller , in remarks yesterday , opened the door to a half-point rate hike next month, though those prospects remain unlikely. As of late Tuesday, CME FedWatch shows a 90.8 percent chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Dec. 9 meeting.

Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson , who wrote the ruling, said the Department of Justice’s attempt to access journalists’ private messages on the networking site also has the potential to expose anonymous sources.

THANK YOU, NEXT: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is wasting no time laying the groundwork for a potential 2028 presidential bid.

He announced yesterday that he penned a new book, called “Next,” which is set to be released on Jan. 26. The former Biden administration official described his new book as “not a policy manual,” but “an account of how we got here and an argument about what could happen if America takes big swings to reform our political system.”

“If we do that, we can have a life that is better, not just better than today, but better than before,” Buttigieg said.

In the book, publisher Simon & Schuster said, Buttigieg “makes the urgent case for seizing the current moment of political rupture as a chance to deliver transformative improvements that the majority of Americans demand” and “lays out a vision for addressing the profound challenges facing our country today.”

Writing a book ahead of a presidential run has become something of a rite of passage for many political candidates — from former President Obama , who wrote “The Audacity of Hope” when he was an Illinois senator, to former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley (R) to Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.).

In 2019, ahead of his run for president in 2020, Buttigieg released a biography, “Shortest Way Home: One Mayor’s Challenge and a Model for America’s Future.”

His publisher did not shy away from hinting at another possible White House bid in its book description: “No matter who the next American president will be, if you are reading ‘Next,’ you are holding our nation’s future in your hands.”

EXXON OVERSEAS: Oil company ExxonMobil has taken a significant step toward returning to Venezuela as Trump has pushed for U.S. oil companies to set up shop in the South American country.

According to The Hill’s Rachel Frazin , the company signed a memorandum of understanding with Venezuela to explore opportunities and locations for where to set up shop.

“This memorandum is a meaningful first step, but any future investment would require stable policies, clear regulations, strong investment protections and competitive returns,” an ExxonMobil spokesperson said on the possibility of moving to the South American nation.

In January, after the U.S. captured Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, Trump said, “We’re going to have our very large United States oil companies, the biggest anywhere in the world, go in, spend billions of dollars, fix the badly broken infrastructure, the oil infrastructure, and start making money for the country.”

Ahead of midterms, Trump continuously called for Venezuela to be the U.S.’s 51st state, while Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez told journalists back in May that the country has no plans of becoming a U.S. territory.

ExxonMobil, alongside ConocoPhillips, were pushed out of the country in 2007 by Venezuelan President Hugo Chávez due to a nationalization push. Chevron, the only oil giant currently operating in the county, is expected to double its production in the coming years.

articles.title: Bessent moved to military base as Iran threats exceed ‘advanced stage,’ official says
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was reportedly relocated to a military base as Iranian assassination plots against U.S. officials intensify.
articles.body: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been relocated from his home in Washington, D.C., to a military base amid Iranian assassination threats this week, a senior administration official confirmed to Fox News. Tehran has ramped up its efforts to target senior U.S. officials overseas, with White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also relocating to military or protected housing in recent weeks. The senior official told Fox that threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage." The official declined to say when exactly Bessent was relocated. Bessent has played a central role in the economic battle against Iran, launching "Operation Economic Outcast" this summer in an effort to isolate Iran's economy from the rest of the world. COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES Bessent said the wave of sanctions would bring about the "asphyxiation" of Iran's economy. The Treasury Department confirmed Bessent's departure in a statement to Fox News on Tuesday, adding that the secretary refuses to "be deterred by the Iranian regime’s threats." The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation, citing three anonymous sources. IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS The move comes as President Donald Trump continues to seek to end the war via diplomatic means, leaning away from a return to full-scale war. Rubio himself downplayed the possibility of re-escalating the conflict on Tuesday. TRUMP MEETS KEY IRAN WAR MEDIATOR AS UAE REVEALS MAJOR OIL EXPORT SURGE DESPITE CONFLICT "We don't need to conduct military strikes if we're achieving the same objective through economic means and economic pressure," Rubio told reporters. He rejected the suggestion that the U.S. and Iran were at a stalemate, arguing that sanctions, the naval blockade and other measures were steadily weakening Tehran. TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN "They’re bleeding. They’re bleeding economically," Rubio said. "It is an increased pressure on Iran that continues to grow every day." The push comes a week after an election in which the war proved a political liability for Republicans. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Iran war was a crucial factor in the House vote for 34% of voters, according to the Fox News Voter Poll, while about six in 10 said the U.S. had made the wrong decision to take military action against Iran. Fox News' Morgan Phillips contributed to this report.

articles.body:
Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom (D) extended his slim lead by more than 3,000 votes over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) ahead of two crucial ballot deadlines in the week after Democrats saw sweeping victories in the midterm elections.

The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ) found that, with around 95 percent of ballots counted, Colom is slightly ahead with 49.11 percent of the vote compared with Hyde-Smith’s 48.79 percent — or 470,266 votes to 467,183, respectively — as of 10:31 p.m. EST.

Independent Senate candidate Ty Perkins holds the third place spot at 2.1 percent of the vote.

These updates come ahead of a Tuesday deadline for provisional ballots and for the receipt of mail-in absentee ballots postmarked by Election Day.

Colom, an attorney, has maintained a narrow lead in one of the biggest surprises of last week’s midterm elections, with the race still too close to call.

On Monday, he called out prominent election forecasters for underestimating his chances of defeating Hyde-Smith in their election ratings, name-dropping the Cook Political Report most notably.

“At some point, we have to talk about … ‘prognosticators’ who had me and other southern candidates labeled as solid R for much of the campaign cycle,” the Democrat wrote on social media .

“They made it much more difficult to fundraise and are part of the reason the South has been neglected for so long,” he continued. “They’re only a reflection of the past and mysteriously avoid any accountability when they’re wrong.”

Despite the numbers, Hyde-Smith has remained optimistic .

The Magnolia State race marks one of two Senate races that have not yet been determined. The Alaska Senate race between Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) is also still open.

Peltola has expanded her own narrow lead over Sullivan as well. The former lawmaker notched 49 percent of the vote to the incumbent’s 47.2 percent as of 11:13 p.m. EST on Tuesday, with 245,470 ballots counted so far, according to unofficial results from Alaska’s Division of Elections.

The state, under ranked-choice voting, will run an instant runoff election if neither candidate collects 50 percent of the first-choice votes, and the process will repeat until a candidate notches the majority.

articles.title: Lawmakers dust off the 27th Amendment in pursuit of back pay
articles.summary: Several members of Congress head to court this week in an under-the-radar lawsuit claiming they’ve been underpaid. It’s a bipartisan issue, with Democrats like Rep. James Clyburn (S.C.) and Republicans like Rep. Rick Crawford (Ark.) joining as plaintiffs. Ratified in 1992, the 27th Amendment says that “no law, varying the compensation” of members of Congress…
articles.body:
Several members of Congress head to court this week in an under-the-radar lawsuit claiming they’ve been underpaid.

It’s a bipartisan issue, with Democrats like Rep. James Clyburn (S.C.) and Republicans like Rep. Rick Crawford (Ark.) joining as plaintiffs.

Ratified in 1992, the 27th Amendment says that “no law, varying the compensation” of members of Congress “shall take effect” until after an election has “intervened.”

Clyburn, Crawford and the others say their colleagues have violated it every time they’ve waived automatic cost-of-living adjustments (COLA) to keep rank-and-file lawmakers’ salaries steady at $174,000 since 2009.

“In every instance, the laws were passed without an election of Representatives beginning and concluding between enactment and that January,” the lawmakers wrote in court filings .

The duo is joined by Rep. Steny Hoyer (D-Md.) and former Reps. Rodney Davis (R-Ill.) and Ed Perlmutter (D-Colo.). Also, it’s a class-action suit, so their colleagues might also be able to cash in on any victory.

That’s right, folks. So don’t let anyone tell you the most recent amendment to the Constitution is a dud.

Ken Cuccinelli , an attorney representing Crawford, said the lawsuit was brought after he and other lawyers “had done a good deal of research” to confirm suspicions that many COLA blocking statutes passed over the last three decades were inconsistent with the amendment.

Eric Bruggink, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims judge mulling it over, gets to be the guinea pig. The appointee of former President Reagan noted it’s a case of first impression and it raises “a complicated web of issues.”

In May, he allowed the lawmakers’ case to proceed but deferred a decision on several other issues. It’s now coming to a head, with arguments set to kick off at 10 a.m. EST on Thursday.

When does an election “intervene” under the amendment?

Is the congressional COLA formula a “law, varying” members’ pay?

If the lawmakers have a valid argument, what years can they seek damages for at this point?

Thanks to partisan fights over the midterms, the judge has some new caselaw to work with to answer that first question.

The government argues that an election has intervened so long as the law was passed before Election Day. The lawmakers say once the first ballot is cast — so, weeks earlier — it’s too late.

Sound familiar? It’s the same debate at the center of Virginia’s redistricting battle that blew up ahead of the midterms.

The Virginia Supreme Court found Democrats didn’t follow the state constitution’s requirement that they pass their map twice, with an election in between, before sending it to voters. Early voting had already begun by the first vote.

The lawmakers say it’s the only judicial decision in American history where the intervening-election requirement is at the core.

They also point to the Supreme Court’s 5-4 decision in June that the federal law scheduling Election Day does not preempt states from accepting mail ballots that arrive days afterward. The lawmakers say the decision confirms the election is the entire period during which the electorate votes.

“But that other line of case law plaintiffs invoke does not compel the inverse: it does not mean that Congress (or the Constitution) has adopted the most expansive time period,” the Justice Department wrote in court filings .

Welcome to The Gavel, The Hill’s weekly newsletter unpacking the intersection of courts & politics from Zach Schonfeld and Sophie Brams . Email us tips at zschonfeld@thehill.com and sbrams@thehill.com . You can also reach out to us on X (@ZachASchonfeld and @sophiebrams) or Signal (zachschonfeld.48 and sbrams.32).

Trump gets border wall win : The Supreme Court will allow border wall construction around Big Bend National Park in Texas to continue while a lawsuit seeking to halt it plays out, handing President Trump another win on the emergency docket.

Special master: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes is tapping former U.S. Attorney Jessie Liu to lead an ethics probe into whether the Trump administration misled her in the ongoing litigation over Trump’s plan to overhaul the golf courses at East Potomac Park in the nation’s capital.

Charlie Kirk’s alleged killer gets trial date: A Utah judge has set a summer 2028 trial date for Tyler Robinson, three years after he was accused of fatally shooting Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk during an event on Utah Valley University’s campus. Kirk’s widow, Erika, called the date “disappointing.”

Trump’s triumphal arch construction paused: U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan has temporarily blocked the Trump administration from moving forward with plans to build a 250-foot arch between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

Sotomayor talks presidential immunity: Justice Sonya Sotomayor said over the weekend that her colleagues had done some “crazy things” and hopes they will revisit a decision granting former presidents broad criminal immunity and overturn it.

Scandal rocks Arkansas Bar: A former Arkansas Supreme Court official has been charged with 65 felony counts for allegedly altering state bar exam scores and deleting supporting records following an investigation into years of scoring irregularities. Dive deeper into the allegations .

Sure, why not: Conservative commentator Hugh Hewitt is making a case for a recent Supreme Court law clerk to be the next White House press secretary. His suggestion ? “A very smart, very articulate lawyer who knows the Constitution inside and out and doesn’t flinch from making arguments based on Article II powers.”

Class is in session : Justice Clarence Thomas is putting on his professor cap. The senior conservative justice is teaching a class called “CIV 166: Equality and the New Birth of Freedom” at the University of Texas in Austin next semester. Read more from Nexstar affiliate KXAN .

A rapid string of resignations has hit the Justice Department following Republicans’ midterm rout, with at least four high-ranking officials exiting in just the last week.

Harmeet Dhillon : head of the Civil Rights Division

Brett Shumate : assistant attorney general for the Civil Division

John Eisenberg : assistant attorney general for the National Security Division

Jason Reding Quiñones : U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida

Dhillon, whose office suffered a string of embarrassing court losses in the Justice Department’s efforts to force states to hand over voter rolls, was the first to go. She insists she wasn’t asked to leave but rather decided weeks ago and was urged by former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to wait until after the election.

Her resignation Thursday was only the beginning. By Friday, Eisenberg and Quiñones had also departed.

Quiñones’s exit likely means the collapse of the administration’s sweeping “grand conspiracy” probe into past criminal investigations of President Trump and his 2016 campaign, which targeted the president’s political enemies.

Shumate resigned Monday, ending his tenure atop the division responsible for defending the president’s most controversial policies in court. Under his direction, the department aggressively pursued legal action against states with sanctuary policies and universities that offered in-state tuition to immigrants who entered the country illegally, among other hot-button culture war issues.

That next day, Trump announced that T. Elliot Gaiser , the head of the Office of Legal Counsel, would be nominated to the federal bench in the North District of Texas.

It’s not unusual for senior officials to leave an administration after midterm elections, especially when the balance of power shifts. But it comes at a time when Democrats are expected to use their newfound majorities in Congress and subpoena power to launch a blitz of oversight investigations next year.

“Lawyer up,” Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, said on election night.

Attorney General Todd Blanche ‘s response?

“This is literally déjà vu all over again,” he told Fox News Sunday. “They’ve tried this before. It didn’t work last time. It’s not going to work this time.”

Democratic control also likely means more hurdles for the Trump administration in trying to confirm permanent replacements.

That may not matter much to Trump though, as he has not shied away from leaning on appointees in temporary roles while their nominations are hung up in Congress.

Cases the Supreme Court is taking up — or passing on — this term.

The Supreme Court granted one new case this past week. Regular Gavel readers saw it coming. We previewed it as one to watch at the start of the term.

This case brings together the world’s most two exciting topics: bankruptcy and arbitration.

Two Apple Card holders who filed for bankruptcy allege that Goldman Sachs kept trying to collect earlier debts from them. (For context, filing for bankruptcy generally places an automatic pause on collection efforts. Violators can be forced to pay the person damages).

The Apple Card agreements had one of those mandatory arbitration clauses you’ve probably seen before. So, Goldman says if the cardholders want to press damages, they need to go to arbitration.

The Supreme Court will decide if that’s true. The case is Goldman Sachs Bank USA v. Brown.

The court turned away dozens of petitions, including baseball legend Roberto Clemente ’s sons’ fight against Puerto Rico officials. The territory made $15 million off license plates branded with imagery of their father. The sons claimed it misappropriated his legacy, but they faced a partial loss in a lower court. The case is Clemente Properties, Inc v. Pierluisi-Urrutia .

The justices asked the Trump administration to weigh in on whether the court should take up AstraZeneca UK v. Atchley , an appeal from pharma companies concerning whether it can be held liable under federal anti-terrorism laws.

It’s the latest company to stare down lawsuits claiming it aided and abetted terrorism in the Middle East and must pay damages under U.S. law. In 2023, the court ruled that Twitter, now called X, wasn’t liable for an ISIS-linked attack in Istanbul several years earlier.

The latest case involves Iraq. Victims killed by the Mahdi Army and their family claim the companies — which include AstraZeneca, Johnson & Johnson and Pfizer, among others — knowingly gave substantial assistance to the attacks by selling pharmaceutical and medical equipment to the Iraqi health ministry.

The companies say they made the sales at the encouragement of the U.S. government, which at the time was making efforts to rebuild the country after the fall of Saddam Hussein .

The Supreme Court often goes with the sitting administration’s recommendation after calling for its views, so this will be one to watch.

Petitions for the Supreme Court to take up cases we are keeping a close eye on this week …

Some of the ones we previewed last week are back again, including Alabama’s redistricting fight. But here are some new additions to our watchlist:

Trump’s asylum ban: This has a strong chance of being the court’s next Trump case. On Inauguration Day, Trump signed a proclamation shutting down asylum processing at the southern border. A lower court ruled that it exceeded federal law, and the administration is appealing. The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services .

Maryland gun law: Like many other states, Maryland restricts carrying firearms in certain locations. That list spans mass transit facilities, schools, casinos, places that sell alcohol, state parks and more. The Supreme Court’s Second Amendment decisions have said that restrictions are permitted in “sensitive places.” But what exactly does that cover? The court could decide in Novotny v. Moore .

Private immigration facilities: The operator of a private immigration detention center is suing over two Washington state laws it says unconstitutionally micromanage its operations. The first regulates conditions at the facility, while the other would force the facility to pay minimum wage to detainees who participate in voluntary work programs. The Trump administration backs the company. The cases are GEO Group Inc. v. Nwauzor and GEO Group Inc. v. Ferguson.

Dogs killed by police: North Las Vegas police killed pit bull mixes who attacked K-9 dogs searching in their backyard for a nearby suspect. The city wants to defeat a lawsuit brought by the owners, who claim a violation of their Fourth Amendment protection against warrantless searches. The city says it was part of a “hot pursuit” and should be protected. The case is City of North Las Vegas v. Jones.

Sprint’s FCC fight: Sprint appeals in its forfeiture fight with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). It’s a similar case to the one the court decided last term concerning Verizon and AT&T. Sprint says the justices can merely just wipe the lower ruling and send it back for another look in light of that, or it can take up the case in full. The case is Sprint Corporation v. FCC .

Securities fraud: Two notable securities-fraud cases are on the list this week. First, Webinar company ON24 wants to defeat claims that it misled investors about financial risks following the COVID-19 pandemic. The court was set to address the issue in a dispute involving Facebook two terms ago, but after taking it up, the court dismissed the case without reaching a ruling. articles.title: The 2026 midterms just ended Israel’s influence over American politics
articles.summary: Standing up to AIPAC’s agenda has become more than just a policy debate. It’s already a moral litmus test in our elections in a way few issues are.
articles.body:
As someone who has spent more than 20 years working for U.S. policies to advance Palestinian rights and freedom, this election night was a moment I sometimes feared I’d never see in my lifetime. Today, I believe I will look back on Nov. 3, 2026, as a turning point in the story of our country and the struggle for human rights for every person around the world.

For decades, criticism of the Israeli government’s treatment of Palestinians, and the ironclad support provided by the U.S., was considered a third rail in politics. Democratic and Republican administrations alike competed to gloat about which side would provide more funding to Israel, regardless of what that meant for Palestinians, whose lives under Israeli military rule got worse each year.

While U.S. public opinion became increasingly supportive of Palestinian human rights and freedom, officials in Washington clung to an old playbook that told them their political future demanded they remain in lockstep with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. They offered platitudes about Palestinians deserving the same rights and freedoms as Israelis. They pledged their support for the two-state solution. Yet year after year, the bombs kept dropping , the land meant for that Palestinian state kept shrinking , and the chasm between what voters wanted and what Congress voted for grew larger.

Last week in Michigan, we saw the beginning of the end of that tragic dynamic. Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in the Democratic Senate primary and now the November general election was historic. He overcame a tidal wave of spending from AIPAC, once a kingmaker in Congress. He overcame shameful bigotry from the highest perches of power in our country, including President Trump, Vice President JD Vance and some members of his own party. He overcame a spectacular betrayal from a Democratic member of Congress .

But his win was also historic because he proved for the first time that a politics of universal human rights that includes Palestinians is a winning platform in the most critical electoral battleground in our country.

Michigan will no doubt again be a decisive state in 2028. Due to a new Democratic primary calendar, it could prove decisive in the contest for the Democratic nominee as well. El-Sayed’s victory has put politicians in both parties on notice because it has made the seismic shift in American public opinion, including in swing states like Michigan, impossible to deny.

An August 2026 Fox News poll found that 55 percent of Michigan voters oppose continuing to provide military funding to the Israeli government. Among Democrats, that figure was 70 percent . Among independents, it was 66 percent. Even among Republicans, 35 percent opposed continuing military funding.

A poll commissioned by my organization, conducted by YouGov in August, found that 80 percent of likely Democratic primary voters in Michigan believe Israel is committing genocide in Gaza. The vast majority of likely Democratic primary voters in the other early-voting states believe this, including 57 percent in South Carolina, 78 percent in Nevada, 78 percent in New Hampshire, 76 percent in New Mexico and 72 percent in Virginia.

It is a new political reality that we have seen play out over the last year, beginning with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s election victory . Since then, champions for Palestinian rights have succeeded against the odds, often in the face of millions of dollars spent against them by AIPAC and its allies, to win primaries in California, Florida, New Jersey, Philadelphia, New York City, Denver and Detroit.

There should be no doubt in anyone’s mind that the question of our country’s relationship to Israel and to Palestinians will define the 2028 Democratic primary for president — and potentially the Republican presidential primary as well.

Trump recently claimed , without providing details, that he would end annual taxpayer funding to Israel’s military, a sign of how toxic that ritual has become. But voter demands go much further. Democratic contenders in particular will have to grapple with a voter base that strongly supports imposing sanctions and stopping all weapons deliveries to Israel, regardless of whether the weapons are paid for by American taxpayers or the Israeli government.

Across party divides, voters are seeing the contradiction between the American people’s interests and the demands of the Israeli government, in part due to Trump’s disastrous decision to launch the Iran war , a longtime goal of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Rising gas prices resulting from the Iran war were top of mind for voters in this midterm election that has cost Republicans both houses of Congress.

For Palestinian Americans like myself, this awakening has been long overdue. We have spent decades trying to explain that Palestinian rights are not a far-away concern. They are a question that gets to the heart of our nation’s commitment to universal human rights and the credibility of our democracy.

It fills us with grief that it took Israel’s killing of more than 70,000 Palestinians in Gaza, including more than 20,000 children , to force the reckoning that might finally bring about real change. Multiple independent United Nations commissions, and many human rights organizations, have determined Israel’s actions in Gaza constitute genocide . The president of the International Court of Justice wrote in 2024 that Israel’s discriminatory laws and measures against Palestinians are “ tantamount to the crime of apartheid .” The American people increasingly agree.

El-Sayed’s victory carries a message for Washington: The bipartisan consensus that has so long denied Palestinians freedom and equality is no longer the consensus of the American people. They want leaders now who will chart a new path that takes Palestinian freedom as its north star.

For those of us who have spent decades fighting to make that possible, this is not the end of the struggle. It is evidence that the struggle has changed our politics for good.

Margaret DeReus is executive director of the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project.

articles.title: New Texas governor-elect strikes conciliatory tone toward Musk after campaigning against SpaceX deal
articles.summary: Gina Hinojosa signaled a possible shift on the Boca Chica State Park land deal, saying Texas can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk.
articles.body: Texas’ Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa is striking a more conciliatory tone toward Elon Musk after campaigning against a proposed SpaceX land deal, saying she can work with his companies if they operate "on our terms." "As Governor, I’ll protect our land and our livelihoods – not sell out to the highest bidder – because Texans deserve a leader who puts the people first," Hinojosa said in a campaign press release in October. But having won her election, her tone has shifted. TED CRUZ SAYS 'BLUE TSUNAMI' TOOK OVER TEXAS AFTER DEMOCRATS SWEPT STATEWIDE RACES The governor-elect has hinted that she might be rethinking her relationship with Musk, underscoring the shifting considerations many Democrats critical of business titans are making as they prepare to govern and secure growth and investments for their constituencies. "We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies," Hinojosa said in an interview with CNN on Thursday, just two days after election night. "But it has to be on our terms. It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that’s what changes now that I will be governor." Hinojosa’s public land concerns center on Boca Chica State Park, a coastal reserve spanning 1,000 acres at the southernmost point of Texas. The park sits just a short distance from SpaceX’s Starbase, one of its rocket launch sites. A possible land sale to Musk has been in the works for some time. A Cameron County Commission agenda notice from 2024 raised a prospect presented by SpaceX: a land swap. Texas would give 43 acres of Boca Chica to SpaceX in return for 477 acres in the nearby area so that the company could expand its launch facilities. In August 2025, the commission approved a separate proposal authorizing TPWD to sell SpaceX four noncontiguous tracts totaling about 1.9 acres. Last year, the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission voted to approve that smaller deal. "The Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission adopts the Resolution attached as Exhibit A and authorizes the Executive Director to take all necessary steps to dispose of four tracts totaling approximately 1.9 acres at Boca Chica State Park," the commission wrote in its agenda records. MUSK ISSUES DIRE WARNING OVER 3 MOVES DEMS COULD MAKE IF THEY SWEEP WASHINGTON: 'END OF DEMOCRACY' During her first press conference after the election, Hinojosa didn’t rule out the project but noted that she had requested that the decision be stayed at least until she took office. "This morning I was pleased to talk to the executive director of the Texas Parks and Wildlife to confirm that this issue was not on today’s agenda and to request that no action be taken out of respect for this transition," Hinojosa said on Thursday. Notably, Hinojosa bashed outgoing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott for even considering the deal with SpaceX, framing it as a capitulation to America’s wealthiest business owner. "After 12 years of selling out Texas to his corporate donors and making working people foot the bill, Greg Abbott is handing over our land to the world’s only trillionaire. Let me be clear: Texas is not for sale," Hinojosa wrote. "This is the One Fight that unites us all: Are we going to be a Texas by and for the people, or is this the billionaires’ world and the rest of us just live here?" Hinojosa’s transition team did not respond to an inquiry from Fox News Digital on whether the governor-elect’s outlook had changed regarding SpaceX or its ongoing negotiations with Texas. It also did not respond to questions about what considerations might prevent Musk from securing the 1.9 acres. Even so, Hinojosa’s language surrounding the land sale seemed to spark blowback from Musk. In a cryptic post to social media, Musk noted that he had relocated his company to Texas because of the state’s commitment to pro-business policies. TEXAS OVERTAKES CALIFORNIA AS 'AMERICA’S CENTER OF GRAVITY,' CLAIMS TREASURY SEC BESSENT "SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government," Musk said in a post to X. "As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas," he added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Having secured her gubernatorial election win over Abbott, Hinojosa will take the oath of office on Jan. 19, 2027.

In an episode…
articles.body:
Donald Trump Jr. is defending Russell Brand following the actor’s conviction on rape and sexual assault charges.

The 51-year-old British comedian and conservative influencer was sentenced Monday in London to more than 10 years in prison for raping a woman and sexually assaulting three others over a five-year period beginning in 2004.

In an episode this week of his Rumble show , “Triggered,” Trump decried what he called the “severe” sentence.

“So when he was like married to Katy Perry, he’s one of the most famous actors in the world, no one seemed to have a problem,” Trump, 48, said of Brand. The performer and “Firework” singer wed in 2010 before splitting a year later.

“No one seemed to think he was a rapist then, but he finds God, I guess, changes his ways, sees some aspects of conservative life, and talks about them. And now he’s going to spend 10 and a half years in prison for rape when no one had a problem with it in the prior 27 years,” Trump said.

Comparing Brand’s sentence to other high-profile cases in Britain, Trump said, “Now, take a step back and think about what this tells you about a society that seems to decide punishment and sentencing based on who you are instead of what you did.”

“The same establishment that lectures America about norms can’t find a consistent sentence for the worst crime on the books,” Trump said.

“Like I always say, it’s just yet another example of how Britain is falling and failing to uphold any sense of equal justice.”

“And again, the stuff that I’ve read with Russell, they were doing some pretty crazy stuff, and then it went further. There were no complaints,” Trump said.

“Then 27 years later, rape. It’s crazy,” he said.

articles.title: Democrats don’t have to choose between affordability and accountability
articles.summary: Americans are in no mood to settle for a party that can only tackle one crisis at a time. If Democrats want to succeed, they’ll need to start treating affordability and accountability as two faces of the same Trumpian corruption crisis.
articles.body:
On Friday, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) drew criticism from some corners of the progressive world when he declined to list impeachment among Democrats’ top priorities for the new congressional term. Jeffries’s affordability-focused comments stood in stark contrast to incoming House Oversight Committee Chair Rep. Robert Garcia’s (D-Calif.) warning that President Trump and Republicans should “ lawyer up ” in preparation for a pile of new corruption investigations.

Writing in The New Republic a few days after Jeffries’s remarks, my friend and progressive stalwart Michael Tomasky worried that Democrats would embrace a “ poisonous ” false choice between prioritizing affordability issues and holding Trump’s lawless regime accountable for its excesses. He’s right: Exit polls found that nearly nine in 10 voters across party lines rated corruption alongside affordability as their top national concern. Those frustrated Americans are in no mood to settle for a party that can only tackle one crisis at a time.

Right now, Jeffries and Democratic leaders are thinking about their priorities as a balancing act between affordability and accountability, treating them as separate issues. Instead, they should be building an approach that uses bold accountability actions to set the stage for serious affordability legislation — and vice versa. That means reframing the problem not as isolated issues but as one sprawling public corruption crisis.

Fortunately for Jeffries and whoever his Senate counterpart turns out to be, the sheer scope of Trump’s graft offers Democrats plenty of opportunities to prove that voters’ affordability woes and Republican corruption walk together. Even better, the lowest-hanging fruit gives Democrats a chance to flex their bipartisanship while at the same time reclaiming for Congress some of the co-equal status Republicans have spent two years ceding to an imperial White House.

Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth were a ripe enough place to start. Hegseth has few defenders and plenty of enemies on Capitol Hill, and a growing number of Republicans publicly blame his mismanagement of the Iran war for dooming their midterm hopes. But those concerns weren’t enough to overcome the GOP’s continued obedience to all things Trump, and on Tuesday night the House voted along party lines to kill Massie’s impeachment effort. If Republicans learned anything from last week’s election blowout, they didn’t show it.

Still, it matters that Democrats forced the issue — and will likely be in a position to bring up Hegseth’s impeachment again in the new term. Hegseth was clearly worried enough about Massie’s impeachment effort that he appeared behind the podium for a rare (for him) Pentagon press briefing that felt more like a defense of his job.

Claiming Hegseth’s scalp before the new Congress is even in session would have been a major boost for Democrats, but his survival reminds voters of exactly the kind of corruption they voted to sweep out of Congress. The GOP’s last, desperate defense of Hegseth won’t stop the tide from turning next year, when newly empowered Democrats are expected to crack down on the Pentagon’s impunity and advance legislation to withdraw congressional support for Trump’s Iran war.

If Hegseth proved to be a missed opportunity, an even better one sits just down the road at the Department of Health and Human Services, where Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is facing a wave of high-profile staff resignations . One former adviser, Calley Means, recently accused Kennedy of public corruption and betraying the “Make America Healthy Again” movement. Democrats have already offered Kennedy the same ultimatum they’ve leveled against Hegseth: resign or face impeachment .

Plenty of Republicans have lost patience with Kennedy’s antics, and his recent visits to Capitol Hill were derailed by high-profile confrontations with Sens. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) and Bill Cassidy (R-La.). Senator-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.) has already backed impeaching Kennedy , and she was joined this week by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Impeachment proceedings would offer Democrats a dual platform to hold Kennedy accountable for his conspiracy theorizing while also platforming the popular health-care reform proposals they championed on the campaign trail.

Democrats have a real opportunity to link affordability and accountability through bold actions that make clear how Trump’s lack of accountability has made life tangibly worse for those Americans who aren’t lucky enough to be MAGA insiders. If they want to succeed, they’ll need to start treating those issues as two faces of the same Trumpian corruption crisis.

Max Burns is a veteran Democratic strategist and founder of Third Degree Strategies.

articles.body:
Editor’s note: This story has been updated to accurately reflect Dan J. Sullivan’s standing in the Alaska Senate race

Former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) on Tuesday surpassed the combined vote total of Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) and independent Dan J. Sullivan following the latest ballot drop in the to-be-determined Senate race.

Peltola expanded her narrow lead over the incumbent, with 49 percent of the vote to the incumbent’s 47.2 percent, as of 11:13 p.m. EST on Tuesday; 84 percent, or 245,470, of the ballots have been counted so far, according to unofficial results from Alaska’s Division of Elections . Dan J. Sullivan received 4,027 votes, or 1.7 percent.

The Alaska Democrat’s lead hit 118,926 to the Sullivans’ unofficial ballot total of 118,703, the records show.

VoteHub’s head of data science, Zachary Donnini, wrote in response to the results on the social platform X that Peltola “now has more votes than both Sullivans combined and a solid chance of reaching 50 percent to avoid [ranked choice voting], and will if the final drops are as blue as they were in the primary.”

The state, under ranked-choice voting, will hold an instant runoff election if neither candidate collects 50 percent of the first-choice votes. The process repeats until a candidate notches the majority.

Peltola’s campaign celebrated the updated results, with campaign manager Cheryl Bruce stating Sen. Sullivan has no “viable path to reelection.”

“We remain exceptionally confident that Mary will be elected when every vote is counted, and Mary is eager to take her fight to the United States Senate,” Bruce said in a statement.

President Trump –– who has questioned the validity of the race ahead of the election and accused Peltola’s campaign of spoiling the vote with Dan J. Sullivan’s inclusion, a claim that she and other Democrats have denied –– posted a graphic on Truth Social of the two Sullivans with their combined vote compared with the Democratic front-runner.

Trump’s graphic has the Sullivans’ vote written in a green font with a check mark, while Peltola’s lead is shown in red with an “X” next to her ballot count.

The fourth-place candidate’s presence on the November ballot angered the Department of Justice (DOJ), which sued to block the certification of the election if the senator lost. The DOJ argued that the spoiler candidate’s name appearing on the ballots could leave Alaskan voters confused . A federal judge dismissed the case .

The race in Alaska, which outlets like the Alaskan Beacon considered a likely win for the Republican incumbent, remains one of the country’s last two Senate races that have yet to be called, with the other being the close race in Mississippi . Senate candidate Scott Colom (D) extended his slim lead by more than 3,000 votes over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.).

Decision Desk HQ, The Hill’s election partner, found Colom leading with 49.11 percent of the vote counted so far to Hyde-Smith’s 48.79 percent — or 470,266 votes to 467,183, respectively — as of 10:31 p.m. EST.

articles.title: Biden says he would not have proceeded with campaign had he known he had cancer
articles.summary: Former President Joe Biden said in an interview released on Wednesday that his debate performance with Donald Trump in 2024 “was not very consequential” and...
articles.body:
Former President Joe Biden said in an interview released on Wednesday that his debate performance with Donald Trump in 2024 "was not very consequential" and that he would have not tried to seek a second term had he known he had cancer.

The interview with PEOPLE comes ahead of the release of Biden's presidential memoir, "Promise Me, America," next week.

The July 2024 debate, in which Biden appeared confused and had difficulty articulating his case for another term, eventually led to the president dropping out of the race and endorsing his vice president, Kamala Harris, just 107 days before the 2024 election.

His debate performance also prompted his wife, first lady Jill Biden, to think the president was having a stroke. But Biden downplayed its influence in the new interview.

"Look, I don't know anybody who hasn't made a mistake in a debate," Biden said in the PEOPLE interview. "To me, it was not very consequential. First of all, I thought there'd be another debate, which there wasn't. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn't another debate, it didn't disturb me because it wasn't consequential."

A planned second debate took place in September, but between Harris and Trump.

Biden would have 'resigned' if he had known about the cancer

The former president was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer just four months after leaving office.

He conceded to having felt "lousy" before knowing about the cancer, and added he would not have attempted to mount another campaign for the White House had he known he was sick.

"If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have resigned. I would've not gone forward, because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running for (president)," he said. "But that wasn't the case … I believe that on an objective basis, I was the best-equipped person to do the job."

He said he let the public know of his diagnosis "when we found out" and denied having hid the truth about his health during his presidency.

"I didn't do that," Biden said. "We let the public know when I found out, when I knew what was going on. I think it's important for a national leader, as president, to let people know they go through some of the very same things that a lot of American people are going through."

Biden's book will be released next Tuesday. He has said his cancer will limit his ability to promote it.
