articles.title: Drug ring busted, illegal aliens cuffed by Homeland Security Task Force in South Carolina: DOJ
articles.summary: A Homeland Security Task Force investigation in South Carolina netted 36 arrests, seizing 346 kilograms of fentanyl and $2.8 million in cash.
articles.body: The Department of Justice on Tuesday announced that dozens of people in South Carolina, including several illegal immigrants, have been arrested in relation to a drug bust and money laundering scheme. A Homeland Security Task Force investigation netted 36 arrests — and nine of the suspects are in the country illegally, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ). The bust resulted in the seizure of 346 kilograms of fentanyl, 23 kilograms of methamphetamine, 70 kilograms of cocaine, 34 pounds of marijuana and 43 firearms. "Nothing will stop the Trump administration’s commitment to protecting the American people from lethal drugs," Attorney General Todd Blanche told Fox News Digital. DOJ ANNOUNCES 81 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS INDICTED AFTER PUERTO RICO DRUG TRAFFICKING TAKEDOWN "Thanks to the work of the Homeland Security Task Force, the people of South Carolina are safer today than they were two years ago. The Department of Justice will continue dismantling drug trafficking networks and delivering justice for victims and their families," he added. Investigators seized $2.8 million in cash and jewelry, 15 luxury vehicles — including two Rolls Royces, a Lamborghini and an Aston Martin — and 17 properties, which the DOJ said is worth $4 million. The drug running operation has been ongoing since at least 2021, and the drugs themselves originated in Mexico. The narcotics were trafficked across the U.S. southern border with Mexico and into South Carolina, according to the DOJ. DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK Notably, members of the ring had infiltrated the prison system in the Palmetto State. "The investigation identified that a Mexico-based drug trafficking and money laundering organization has been operating in South Carolina since at least 2011 and its members are active in Mexico, South Carolina, other states, as well as within the Bureau of Prisons and South Carolina Department of Corrections," according to the DOJ. The Homeland Security Task Force was assembled under Executive Order 14159, dubbed "Protecting the American People Against Invasion," and is described as a "whole-of-government partnership dedicated to eliminating criminal cartels, foreign gangs, transnational criminal organizations, and human smuggling and trafficking rings operating in the United States and abroad." "Today's indictment sends a clear message that law enforcement will continue pursuing those responsible for distributing dangerous drugs and fueling criminal activity in our communities," said Michael J. Connolly, acting special agent in charge of the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) Atlanta Field Division. "This investigation reflects the dedication and coordinated efforts of our federal, state, and local partners. We will not stop at the first arrest. We will continue following the evidence, identifying those involved, and holding them accountable." FEDS DISMANTLE ALLEGED GUN TRAFFICKING RING THAT FUNNELED DOZENS OF FIREARMS FROM GEORGIA TO CHICAGO GANGS No fewer than 29 law enforcement agencies were involved in the investigation, including the DEA, FBI, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), state investigators in South Carolina and police departments in North and South Carolina.

articles.title: Moderate Dem governor-elect in hot seat after signaling one of her 'top priorities' in presser: 'Resist'
articles.summary: Amy Klobuchar's push for Minnesota gun safety legislation drew fierce conservative backlash over a bill that would ban AR-15 sales and limit magazines.
articles.body: Minnesota Governor-elect Amy Klobuchar, who has positioned herself as a moderate during her years in Congress, is facing blowback over comments made shortly after the election suggesting she will push for gun control when she takes office. "The gun safety bill is going to get passed, and I am so excited to be working with the leaders on this, and it certainly should be one of our top priorities," Klobuchar said during a press conference. "I think that bill makes a lot of sense. I’m sure that we’ll make some changes … but the basics of that bill I hope will remain in place." The bill Klobuchar referenced is SF 4067, an omnibus gun-control package that passed the Minnesota Senate 34-33 earlier this year but has not received a House vote. The measure would prohibit federally licensed firearms dealers from selling certain semiautomatic military-style assault weapons, including AR-15s, as well as large-capacity magazines capable of holding more than 17 rounds. The legislation would allow current owners to keep the covered firearms and magazines, but require them to obtain an ownership certification from the state Bureau of Criminal Apprehension and renew that certification every three years. Knowingly possessing an uncertified weapon or magazine would be a gross misdemeanor, with a subsequent violation punishable as a felony. INSIDE TRUMP'S UNPRECEDENTED BATTLE PLAN TO EXPAND SECOND AMENDMENT RIGHTS THROUGH JUSTICE DEPARTMENT Klobuchar quickly faced criticism from conservatives and pro-Second Amendment groups on social media, accusing her of pushing a liberal gun control agenda on law-abiding Minnesotans, particularly in rural areas. "Democrats don't care about affordability. They only care about taking away our Second Amendment rights," conservative communicator Steve Guest posted on X. "Amy Klobuchar can't contain her excitement as she goes after law-abiding gun owners." "In one of her first acts as governor-elect, Sen. @amyklobuchar affirmed that she will go after Minnesotans' firearms under the guise of ‘safety,’" the National Rifle Association (NRA) posted on X. "When Amy Klobuchar told you over and over she was going to do a top-to-bottom audit, she meant of your guns, not your tax dollars," Minnesota attorney and former immigration judge Nathan Hansen posted on X. Minnesota Miners, a pro-mining grassroots nonprofit in Minnesota, posted on X. "Instead you should be coming out with your plan to stop government fraud and lowering taxes. But you can't do that you have to come out attacking & trying to violate lawful gun owners constitutional rights." "We have a duty to our nation to not comply," Minnesota Republican state Rep. Ben Davis posted on X. "Resist." "AMY KLOBUCHAR ISN'T EVEN SWORN IN AND SHE'S ALREADY COMING FOR MINNESOTA'S RIFLES," conservative influencer Gunther Eagleman posted on X. "I am committed as ever to moving our state forward, not moving our state to the left or to the right, but moving our state forward," Klobuchar said during the press conference. Klobuchar, who has served as a Minnesota senator since 2007, defeated Minnesota Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth 13 points in the gubernatorial election earlier this month and will take office in January, replacing Gov. articles.title: Democrats won — how much can they do now to restrain Trump?
articles.summary: As the country prepares for congressional investigations and possibly impeachments, the Supreme Court’s Trump-friendly majority is poised again to put its thumb on the constitutional scale in two instances.
articles.body:
Although last week’s midterm results were a colossal win for Democrats across legislative and gubernatorial offices, it didn’t change the configuration of the U.S. Supreme Court — which has much to answer for when it comes to the chaos, corruption, and carnage of the second Trump administration.

Since it invented criminal immunity for presidents in June of 2024, the court’s 6-3 majority has handed President Trump wins in eighty percent of his so-called “emergency” petitions for relief — the emergency usually being that the lower courts, applying the law and the Constitution, had impeded Trump from doing what he wanted when he wanted.

As the country prepares for congressional investigations and possibly impeachments of Trump officials, the Trump family, and even Trump himself, the court’s Trump-friendly majority is poised again to put its thumb on the constitutional scale in two instances.

First, the Supreme Court could help Trump if asked to weigh in on lawsuits involving congressional investigations. The landslide victories for Democrats mean that accountability is coming, but there’s only so much Congress can do. It can pass legislation, but the new House and Senate majorities are not veto-proof . Without substantial Republican support, Senate Democrats lack the 67 votes needed to remove Trump or his Cabinet officials through impeachment. Even if they could pass new legislation to rein in Trump’s worst excesses, for nearly two years now, he has shown little hesitation in violating statutory law while defying court orders with impunity.

What Democrats in Congress can do is block his judicial and executive branch nominees; control committees; pass certain budget reconciliation legislation; conduct investigations, issue subpoenas and hold hearings. Congress doesn’t have its own law enforcement apparatus, so if the individuals aligned with the Trump administration defy subpoenas or even lie under oath, it is up to the Department of Justice to pursue criminal contempt referrals from Congress. Attorney General Todd Blanche will undoubtedly continue to side with lawlessness at Trump’s behest rather than do his actual job by upholding the rule of law.

Congress does have the power to bring civil contempt cases in federal court, although that route is slow and laborious. In 2019, three House of Representatives committees issued congressional subpoenas to Trump’s accounting firm and financial institutions in connection with money laundering and related legislation. Trump sued in his individual capacity to block the subpoenas, arguing that they violated the separation of powers. In a 7-2 ruling , the Supreme Court held that Congress doesn’t have unlimited power to subpoena private records from a sitting president, noting that “without limits on its subpoena powers, Congress could … aggrandize itself at the president’s expense.”

That case, Trump v. Mazars, came down before the court’s criminal immunity ruling in Trump v. U.S., in which the majority vastly expanded presidential power by declaring certain “core” powers effectively above the law, and “official” authority presumptively immune from criminal scrutiny even if employed to commit crimes. In Mazars, moreover, Trump didn’t even assert executive privilege.

Taken together, if Team Trump snubs or even obstructs Congress’s oversight efforts and a case goes to the Supreme Court, there is a real chance that the majority will apply these recent precedents in Trump’s favor once again.

Second, the court is essentially taking up the question of whether presidents can bypass the Constitution through private parties. Trump gave Elon Musk unprecedented authority over a slew of federal agencies through his creation of the Department of Government Efficiency by executive order (Congress has the constitutional authority to create agencies, not presidents). Musk wasn’t appointed under Article II of the Constitution or confirmed by the Senate, either. The same goes for Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who has been trotting around the globe purportedly negotiating peace in the Middle East and Ukraine on behalf of the American public on an allegedly volunteer basis. At the same time, he has gotten exponentially richer .

Regarding DOGE, litigants sued under the Freedom of Information Act to obtain basic information about its organizational structure and access to sensitive governmental systems, such as the Social Security Administration. The lower court ruled that DOGE was not exempt from FOIA and that certain records must be turned over. On an emergency petition, a 6-3 Supreme Court stayed that ruling last year, emphasizing that judges should exercise restraint when it comes to executive branch communications.

The court has since taken up parts of that case this term. If the court agrees with Trump that discovery into DOGE’s structure, authority and operations is not permissible, it would undoubtedly invite future presidents to gift governmental power to private actors without oversight. If that were to happen, Congress would have to act urgently to confine the likes of Musk and Kushner within the rule of law.

The good news for those concerned about the overbearing power of the Supreme Court is that the new Senate majority can block another Trump nominee, as then-Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) did to President Barack Obama’s nomination of Merrick Garland in 2016 .

If a Democrat wins the White House in 2028, replacing just two conservative justices could flip the right wing of the court from six justices to four, ushering in a new progressive era. The Constitution would be better off for it.

Kimberly Wehle is currently a thematic group coordinator and fellow at the Netherlands Institute for Advanced Study in the Humanities and Social Sciences and author of “How to Read the Constitution — and Why,” as well as “What You Need to Know About Voting — and Why” and “How to Think Like a Lawyer — and Why. “

articles.title: White House pushes back on Democrats, saying investigations could ‘cross the line’ into crime
articles.summary: The White House has floated that it may seek to investigate the investigators in the incoming Congress, writing Monday in a letter to Democrats on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee that their probes “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” The letter showcases the Trump administration’s aggressive stance toward coming investigations from congressional…
articles.body:
The White House has floated that it may seek to investigate the investigators in the incoming Congress, writing Monday in a letter to Democrats on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee that their probes “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The letter showcases the Trump administration’s aggressive stance toward coming investigations from congressional Democrats, who will wield subpoena power when the party retakes control of both chambers of Congress in January.

“Compulsory process is a power Congress has for oversight functions, and only for oversight functions. Abusive threats and public statements about the indiscriminate issuance of subpoenas, along with threats directed at prospective targets within the Administration make it abundantly clear that any forthcoming investigative processes will be deployed to harass and aggrandize, rather than to advance any legitimate legislative end,” White House counsel Will Scharf wrote to incoming House Oversight Chair Robert Garcia (D-Calif.).

Scharf asserted that any subpoenas “designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient” could be criminal, while “issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”

The letter was first reported by Punchbowl Nes.

Garcia has sought to make a splash as Democrats retake committee gavels. The night of the election, he issued only a two-word statement, telling administration officials to “lawyer up.”

On Wednesday he pushed back against Scharf’s letter, asserting they were operating well within the bounds of the law.

“It appears Donald Trump has something to hide. Let’s be clear: Congress’ authority comes from Article I of the Constitution, not from the permission of the White House. Congress has wide latitude to conduct investigations and oversight, an authority inherent in the power to legislate,” he said in a statement.

“The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse. The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”

A spokeswoman for Garcia, Sara Guerrero, later shared on X that the committee had yet to actually receive the letter.

Scharf’s letter was swiftly blasted as overreach, with attorneys noting that lawmakers are protected by the Speech and Debate Clause for actions taken within their legislative role. They also note it’s a crime to obstruct congressional investigations.

The move could also backfire, as Democrats may determine they are better off quickly issuing subpoenas rather than negotiating over terms with a White House that has signaled its plans to rebuff their investigations.

Scharf has argued Congress must have a legitimate legislative purpose underpinning any subpoena. In recent years, as Republicans requested documents related to the criminal investigations into President Trump, they asserted they may draft laws to limit such probes.

Democrats have already launched a series of probes into what they say is likely corruption from Trump and his family members.

Garcia’s committee has sent recent letters inquiring about the business ventures of Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and former U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle’s texts pleading for money from Trump allies to pay off credit card debt. Multiple committees have sought information about Trump’s crypto ventures, and they plan to pursue cases where they say he has profited from the presidency. That also includes issuing pardons to major donors.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been accused of improperly using the levers of power to launch its own investigations into perceived foes of the president.

The Justice Department has brought cases against former FBI Director James Comey, as well as New York Attorney General Letitia James (D).

But they’ve also seen many of their efforts thwarted by grand juries, who have taken the highly unusual step of rejecting several proposed indictments, including recently for former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson. In February, a grand jury rejected an effort to bring charges against six Democratic lawmakers for a video reminding service members they may refuse to carry out illegal orders.

articles.body:
A House Education and Workforce subcommittee will weigh the rise of sports gambling on campuses amid growing concerns about student-athlete safety and the integrity of college sports.

The hearing comes as the NCAA faces mounting pressure to address gambling-related scandals, harassment of athletes and wagers tied to individual player performances. Congress is also weighing the bipartisan Protect College Sports Act, which passed the Senate in September but faces an uncertain future in the House.

The association has pushed for restrictions on so-called prop bets involving college athletes, warning that such wagers can expose players to harassment and potential manipulation.

The hearing is scheduled to begin at 10:15 a.m. EST.

articles.title: ‘He blamed the Jews’: GOP congressman levels explosive accusation against JD Vance over election postmortem
articles.summary: Rep. Randy Fine compared JD Vance's post-midterm election analysis to 1932 Germany, saying the vice president tacitly blamed Jewish people for GOP losses.
articles.body: Rep. Randy Fine, R-Fla., said Vice President JD Vance's election analysis posted online last week amounted to an attack on the Jewish people, leading him to swear off support for any presidential aspirations Vance might have for 2028. "I definitively will not be supporting the vice president in that nominating contest. I thought his message that he put out the day after the election was abhorrent and, frankly, smacked of the kind of thing you’d read in 1932 Germany," Fine, who is himself Jewish, said in an interview with Fox Now. "He’s out in my book," he added. "He blamed the Jews for losing the election." VANCE COURTING DISGRUNTLED TRUMP VOTERS TO FORM ‘NEW RIGHT’ ALLIANCE AFTER REPUBLICAN BLOODBATH, SOURCES SAY Fine’s blistering attack on Vance comes as the GOP is working to understand the midterm election results, in which Republicans lost control of the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate. It also underscores tensions in the GOP as the party wrestles with how to balance America-First principles with its alliance with Israel. In his breakdown, Vance cited polling that identified four key items disillusioned voters wanted to see from Republicans: ending the war in Iran, focusing on the cost of living, putting America first and changing the U.S.-Israel relationship. "Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats," Vance wrote. Amid that mix, Vance especially singled out the first item, noting that Trump had himself identified the Iran conflict as a decisive factor in the midterms in interviews after the election. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance said. "The president himself said so last night." But Fine had a different diagnosis. When asked about his comments by Fox News Digital, Fine doubled down on his characterization, arguing that the vice president had tacitly laid blame on "the Jews" in three of the four reasons he had identified. RUBIO'S DEFENSE OF TRUMP'S IRAN WAR DRAWS SHARP CONTRAST WITH VANCE'S MIDTERM BLAME "What does America First mean when you've said, ‘end the war’ and ‘change our relationship with Israel?’ Isn't that saying the same thing? When you hear… talk about America First, are they saying, ‘let's stop giving aid to Egypt?’ No, it's always about Israel. So it's three times out of four things," Fine said. Although Vance’s election breakdown didn’t mention Jews specifically, Fine believes the connection between Israel as a state and the Jewish people is inseparable. "You can't be Jewish if you don't believe in Israel. It's core to our identity and who we are," Fine said. Fine also believes there is a distinction between Trump’s view of the war in Iran and the breakdown expressed by Vance. In particular, Fine highlighted comments from Trump in which the president said he would likely do the war over again if given the opportunity. "The president said it himself. He said, I would do it again knowing what I know now because they can't have a nuclear weapon," Fine said. "I'm not sure JD Vance is bothered by the idea of Iran having a nuclear weapon," he added. Vance’s office declined to respond to the characterization. ROBERT L MAGINNIS: IRAN WAR COST REPUBLICANS CONGRESS. WHAT WILL IT COST AMERICA? Fine has been one of Israel’s loudest supporters in the House of Representatives. He has introduced several pro-Israel pieces of legislation, such as the Enhanced Iran Sanctions Act of 2025, argued that the U.S. should recognize the Muslim Brotherhood, a political-religious organization, as a terrorist organization, and urged the U.S. to officially designate the Palestinian-controlled West Bank with the Jewish historical names of "Judea and Samaria." He encouraged Republicans to steer clear of seeing Israel as the reason why the GOP underperformed in the midterm elections. articles.title: The high cost of Trump’s $1 coin
articles.summary: he U.S. has long avoided putting images of people living on their currency, and for good reason.
articles.body:
Earlier this year, the Department of the Treasury issued a $1 Trump coin for the American semiquincentennial. While a coin bearing a sitting president’s image may seem harmless, it establishes a dangerous precedent, weaponizing the U.S. Mint for personal political branding.

The United States has historically had a love-hate relationship with $1 coins. The Coinage Act of 1792 established a federal mint to produce U.S. currency. The Civil War precipitated the issuance of greenbacks paper currency to finance the war. The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 launched the nation’s banking system, with the Federal Reserve Board issuing the first federal note, a $10 in 1914 . Yet even as paper became the standard, the government repeatedly tried to force a return to coinage.

Based on the ill-conceived plan to phase out the $1 banknote, the Native American One Dollar Coinage Act of 2009 ramped up the minting of $1 coins for circulation. In 2011, around 1.4 billion such coins were in storage in Federal Reserve vaults . Given that the cost effectiveness of introducing $1 coins for general circulation was debunked, many of these coins continue to sit in storage in Federal Reserve vaults , with little demand for them.

The $1 coin has never gained widespread acceptance in the US . Americans like their $1 banknotes, no matter how low its buying power sinks . Canada did away with their $1 banknote in 1989 , replacing it with their “ loonie ” $1 coin. They even did away with $2 banknotes in 1996 , replacing it with the “ toonie ” coin. The European Union’s smallest banknote denomination is five euros , while the United Kingdom’s smallest banknote is five pounds . Though living leaders do appear on these currencies, such as the UK and Canada, they signify constitutional monarchies , while the U.S. is a constitutional republic .

The U.S. Mint produced $1 coins as part of the Presidential $1 Coin Program , which has now been terminated , replaced by the American Innovation Dollars program that will run through 2032. The requirement is that any person depicted must be deceased for at least two years before the coin is issued. The George H.W. Bush coin , for instance, was issued in 2020, two years after he died . Given the death of Jimmy Carter on Dec. 29, 2024 , we can expect that a $1 coin will be issued bearing his image sometime after Dec. 29, 2026. These coins are generally not issued for circulation, but rather for numismatists , or people who collect coins.

The U.S. Mint has taken advantage of this numismatic market. In 2024, they sold $469 million in numismatic products , the majority of which will never get circulated. They also sold more than $2.3 billion in bullion coins (made of silver, gold or platinum), which serve as vehicles for investment in such metals.

So will a Trump coin shift this aversion to $1 coins among consumers? Hardly. While legally designated under a circulating program, the Mint distributes them primarily to collectors. As a commemorative item, collectors will buy it to add to their collection. Beyond that, it offers no practical purpose.

It is this lack of economic utility that uncovers the coin’s true intent. Given that the coin does not fill any practical need, its creation becomes entirely political. Indeed, the issue is far bigger than just the coin itself.

The U.S. has long avoided putting images of people living on their currency . There is good reason for this policy; countries that feature living presidents on their currency either are dictatorships or have a monarch . Kim Jong Il is depicted on North Korea’s 5000 won note . Saddam Hussein was on Iraq’s currency during his presidency. In contrast, France and South Korea deliberately reject the practice of printing living leaders on money, to ensure that national currency represents the permanent state rather than a temporary ruler.

Having a sitting president on a U.S. coin sets a bad precedent and places our nation in unfavorable company. This practice is also associated with a monarch, something that the “ No Kings ” protests railed against.

This pattern extends beyond money — the administration’s push to build a 250-foot triumphal arch also reeks of personal branding. Just as the Treasury used legal loopholes to mint the sitting president’s face, the executive branch relied on a 1925 law to justify an architectural monument without congressional consent . This overreach triggered a federal judge to issue a temporary restraining order blocking the project.

Given that the Treasury Department appears willing to do just about anything that the president asks, the Trump $1 coin was issued using the Circulating Collectible Coin Redesign Act of 2020 in commemoration of the nation’s 250th anniversary. This effectively bypasses the “two years after death” rule by placing Trump’s image on the obverse side of the coin. The Treasury’s legal justification relies on a single exception, the 1926 Sesquicentennial half-dollar featuring sitting President Calvin Coolidge .

Yet the symbolism of doing so signals personal political branding, not the actions of a public servant working for the nation’s greater good. Indeed, the optics of executive overreach serve as a red flag of the work ahead for the new Congress, including passing a permanent ban on minting living politicians. Independent of each members’ party affiliation, when the legislative branch shirks its responsibility to place guardrails on executive power, the foundation of our government begins to erode — in this case, one dollar at a time.

Sheldon H. Jacobson, Ph.D., is a professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He applies his expertise in data-driven risk-based decision-making to evaluate and inform public policy.

articles.title: Ben Ferguson: ‘My name has been floated’ as next White House press secretary
articles.summary: Conservative commentator and talk show host Ben Ferguson said he might be in the running to become the White House’s next press secretary, saying he knew his name “has been floated.” During an appearance on Fox News, when asked whether he is up for the job, Ferguson said, “Look, my name has been floated around…
articles.body:
Conservative commentator and talk show host Ben Ferguson said he might be in the running to become the White House’s next press secretary, saying he knew his name “has been floated.”

During an appearance on Fox News, when asked whether he is up for the job, Ferguson said, “Look, my name has been floated around there. … I haven’t talked to the president directly about this.”

“I would say this: If the president calls and offers me the job, I would be honored to serve the president,” he added.

Over the weekend , President Trump talked about offering the job to Dana White, who is president and CEO of UFC. The president also requested White bring “assistants” with him and named several UFC fighters.

The next day , he told reporters that he “was only kidding.”

“Of course, I was kidding. And you can see that, because they put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with them. But it was, it was just a little fun,” Trump added.

White then showed up in the White House briefing room with Trump on Monday as the president took questions from reporters.

The search for White House’s next press secretary has been underway after political commentator Katie Zacharia left the position last month following scrutiny about her qualifications and performance.

Zacharia, whose tenure lasted five days , had a rough start when her first press briefing lasted 14 minutes. She took questions from three conservative-leaning outlets and announced the departure of Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece.

Her job history was also brought into question as she previously claimed she was a lawyer, and reports surfaced about her not being licensed to practice law in any state.

She filled the position after her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, left the administration earlier this year.

articles.title: Multiple Kennedy family members seek to join legal battle against Trump's triumphal arch
articles.summary: Kennedy family members are seeking to join legal actions challenging plans to build President Donald Trump's triumphal arch, which he wants built in Washington, D.C.
articles.body: Nine members of the Kennedy family sought on Tuesday to join litigation opposing President Donald Trump's bid to build a triumphal arch in the nation's capital. "President Donald J. Trump is attempting to unlawfully erect a massive arch that will permanently cast shadows over and damage historically significant sightlines to the existing gravesites and memorials established in the Kennedy family’s honor at Arlington National Cemetery, as well as to the memorials of hundreds of thousands of fallen American heroes," their complaint asserted. FEDERAL JUDGE TEMPORARILY BLOCKS CONSTRUCTION OF TRUMP'S ARLINGTON TRIUMPHAL ARCH HOURS AFTER APPROVAL "The plaintiffs include Rory Kennedy, Maxwell Kennedy, Christopher G. Kennedy, Kerry Kennedy, Courtney Kennedy, the Hon. Kathleen Kennedy Townsend, and the Hon. Joseph P. Kennedy II, children of Sen. Robert F. Kennedy and Ethel Kennedy; the Hon. Joseph P. Kennedy III, a grandchild of Robert and Ethel Kennedy; and Edward M. Kennedy, Jr., son of Sen. Edward M. Kennedy," according to a Democracy Defenders Fund press release. Rory and Maxwell Kennedy discussed the issue in a statement on the family's behalf. "This action is about protecting sacred spaces that belong to the American people. Our parents, Robert and Ethel Kennedy, and our uncles, President John F. Kennedy and Senator Edward M. Kennedy, are laid to rest at Arlington National Cemetery. Our uncle Joseph P. Kennedy Jr., who lost his life serving our country in World War II, is also memorialized there. They are among the more than 400,000 veterans and family members buried or honored on this hallowed ground. We believe Donald Trump has violated the laws and procedures established by Congress to protect this most sacred national memorial. In bringing this lawsuit, we stand for those who can not stand for themselves. LAWYER SAYS 250-FOOT TRUMP ARCH DISRUPTS HISTORIC SIGHTLINES CHERISHED BY VETERANS SEEKING BURIAL AT ARLINGTON "Americans from every corner of the country visit Arlington to honor those who served and sacrificed for our nation. A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come. Our lawsuit asks the administration to respect the sanctity of Arlington National Cemetery, the laws established to protect it, and the rights of all Americans who come here to honor those who have served our country," the family's statement said. Last week, a federal judge temporarily blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on the proposed triumphal arch, shortly after a federal planning commission approved the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day temporary restraining order halting construction. White House spokesman Davis Ingle issued this statement on Wednesday to Fox News Digital: "An activist district court has temporarily blocked the construction of the long-awaited Arch. It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery. The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation. We will continue making the case for this beautiful and fitting monument and are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds. We look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch—a tribute to 250 years of American greatness." Trump has said the arch would be utilized for military purposes. Fox News Digital's Michael Sinkewicz contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump declares ‘huge victory’ after judge allows suit against BBC to proceed
articles.summary: President Trump celebrated a federal judge’s decision on Tuesday to permit his defamation case against the BBC to proceed. The president called U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz’s ruling “a Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth” in a Truth Social post. In the Tuesday ruling, the Trump-appointed judge denied in…
articles.body:
President Trump celebrated a federal judge’s decision on Tuesday to permit his defamation case against the BBC to proceed.

The president called U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz’s ruling “a Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth” in a Truth Social post .

In the Tuesday ruling, the Trump-appointed judge denied in part the British network’s attempt to dismiss the president’s $10 billion lawsuit. Trump is suing the BBC over its decision to edit together two different parts of his speech ahead of the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

“Accepting the allegations in the complaint as true, the Court finds Trump plausibly pled damages where Trump alleges a defamatory documentary released toward the election caused reputational harm,” Kuntz wrote in his ruling.

The edited clip, which was included in a BBC documentary, omitted a section of his remarks in which Trump told his supporters to march “peacefully and patriotically.”

“On its face, the editing may independently establish the plausibility of actual malice,” Kuntz wrote in the ruling. “BBC tries to frame this editing as ordinary editing done to condense a seventy-minute-long speech into twelve seconds. But the Court is not persuaded.”

The network has since apologized for airing the speech compilation and ousted several senior leadership officials following the president’s lawsuit.

“We will continue fighting against, and defeating, all of those who try to deceive the American People!” the president wrote Tuesday.

Last month, a federal judge ordered that Trump testify in the case before Dec. 11 or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit.

The president was previously scheduled to sit for a deposition in October, but the network said Trump’s attorneys informed it he was unable to appear by this date “due to other matters of national importance.”

A BBC spokesperson said in a Tuesday statement they were “surprised” by the new ruling but emphasized “respect” for Kuntz’s authority over the matter.

“We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process,” the spokesperson said, according to the British broadcaster .

articles.title: Jordi Wild carga contra Vox tras cancelar Abascal su entrevista: "Estoy profundamente decepcionado"
articles.standfirst: El creador de contenido explica por qué Vox canceló a última hora la entrevista de Santiago Abascal en 'The Wild Project'
articles.summary: El creador de contenido explica por qué Vox canceló a última hora la entrevista de Santiago Abascal en 'The Wild Project'
articles.body: Santiago Abascal no acudirá finalmente a 'The Wild Project'. La entrevista que el líder de Vox tenía previsto grabar este miércoles con Jordi Wild ha sido cancelada por decisión de la formación política, una decisión que ha provocado numerosas críticas en redes sociales. Horas después del anuncio, el propio creador de contenido ha publicado un vídeo para explicar lo sucedido, dar su versión de los hechos y mostrar su decepción con el partido y con el propio Abascal. "Estoy profundamente decepcionado con Vox, con el equipo de Abascal y con el propio Santiago", comienza explicando. Jordi Wild asegura que la cancelación se produjo de manera unilateral y con muy poco margen de tiempo, cuando llevaba días preparando una conversación que formaba parte de un proyecto especial de entrevistas a los principales candidatos políticos. El creador de contenido tenía previsto entrevistar a Ada Colau, Pedro Sánchez, Alberto Núñez Feijóo y Santiago Abascal. Las conversaciones estaban programadas para publicarse este viernes, 13 de noviembre, coincidiendo con el inicio de la campaña electoral. Sin embargo, la decisión de Vox ha impedido completar las cuatro entrevistas previstas. "Si hubiera querido venir, estaría aquí. De eso no hay ninguna duda", afirma Jordi Wild, que considera que el líder de Vox tenía capacidad para desbloquear la situación si realmente hubiera querido mantener el compromiso. En su explicación, Jordi Wild detalla que desde el principio había establecido unas condiciones comunes para los cuatro candidatos. El objetivo era garantizar que las entrevistas se publicasen completas y sin modificaciones posteriores. Para ello, había preparado un contrato que todos los políticos aceptaron firmar, incluido el equipo de Vox, aunque, según cuenta, inicialmente se mostró reticente. "Me comprometía legalmente a no tocar ni un solo píxel de la entrevista, que se iba a publicar íntegra y que, a cambio, solo pedía que ellos no me exigieran ningún tipo de recorte, cambio, etcétera", explica. La situación cambió el martes por la tarde, después de que Abascal acudiera a 'La Revuelta'. Según el relato de Jordi Wild, el equipo de Vox se puso en contacto con él para comunicarle que quería firmar un nuevo contrato que garantizase que no se modificaría el contenido. El creador de contenido asegura que aceptó revisar y firmar otro documento sin ningún problema. Sin embargo, posteriormente recibió una nueva exigencia: "Ahora quieren ellos grabar la entrevista y quieren que sea suya". Según explica, el partido pretendía hacerse con los derechos audiovisuales y tener el control del material. "Esto es absolutamente imposible, es una falta de respeto a mi profesionalidad", sostiene. Jordi Wild insiste en que no tenía ningún interés en editar o manipular las respuestas de Abascal y que incluso estaba dispuesto a permitir que el equipo del político acudiese con sus propias cámaras y grabadoras. Durante la conversación con el jefe de campaña de Vox, según relata, también apareció repetidamente la polémica de la entrevista de Abascal con David Broncano. El equipo del partido le trasladó su malestar porque, según su versión, 'La Revuelta' había eliminado cerca de 40 minutos de la conversación. Jordi Wild respondió que aquella situación no tenía por qué afectar a su proyecto: "¿Qué tiene que ver Broncano conmigo? Yo soy otro mundo, yo no soy una productora, yo no soy una cadena de televisión". El creador de contenido también ha compartido su interpretación personal de lo ocurrido. Considera que la entrevista en 'The Wild Project' podía resultar más complicada para Abascal después de su paso por el programa de TVE, donde, a su juicio, el líder de Vox había salido reforzado ante parte del público. "Después de salir tan reforzado de 'La Revuelta', porque evidentemente, aunque estén muy enfadados porque les han cortado cosas, salen muy reforzados de imagen, sobre todo con el público joven, venir aquí era un riesgo", afirma. Jordi Wild explica que tenía preparadas preguntas sobre cuestiones económicas y de política exterior con las que pretendía poner al dirigente político en una situación incómoda y pedirle explicaciones sobre algunas de sus propuestas. No obstante, deja claro que se trata de una interpretación personal y que no dispone de pruebas para asegurar que ese fuera el motivo de la cancelación. "Mi sensación es que lo que quieren, después de que haya ido bien lo de Broncano, es minimizar riesgos", señala. También contempla la posibilidad de que el equipo jurídico de Vox haya sido quien haya tomado la decisión definitiva. El presentador insiste en que la entrevista habría sido exigente, pero respetuosa. "Hubiera sido tratado con respeto, educación y como un ser humano", asegura.

articles.title: Almost half of MAGA Trump supporters call movement a loser in midterms: Survey
articles.summary: Nearly half of MAGA supporters say their movement was a loser in the midterms, according to a new poll. In a new poll from Politico, 45 percent of MAGA supporters of President Trump said the movement was the loser in last week’s election results, while 59 percent of respondents overall said the same. Thirty-four percent…
articles.body:
Nearly half of MAGA supporters say their movement was a loser in the midterms, according to a new poll .

In a new poll from Politico, 45 percent of MAGA supporters of President Trump said the movement was the loser in last week’s election results, while 59 percent of respondents overall said the same. Thirty-four percent of MAGA supporters identified Trump as a loser for the election, while 62 percent of respondents overall said the same.

The poll comes after Republicans experienced a shellacking in the midterms last week, losing control of both the House and Senate. The GOP also notably lost in places like Texas and Kansas, where Democrats have historically struggled.

Republicans faced an uphill battle during this year’s midterms, with issues like the unpopular Iran war, Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living weighing the GOP down as they headed into Election Day.

On Election Day, Trump’s approval rating sat at 38.4 percent, while his disapproval rating was 58.7 percent, according to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ.

Republicans came back to Washington this week in the wake of their blowout loss in a negative mood. The blue wave of this year’s midterms has resulted in a reckoning for the GOP and brought up questions about what went wrong for the party.

On Monday, Trump asked how polls could have been “so wrong” following Democrats’ midterm wins and raised questions about if the elections were “honest.”

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The Politico poll took place from Nov. 7-10, featuring 2,000 respondents and a margin of error of 2 percentage points.

articles.title: Bernie Sanders says he won't back Schumer as push for new leadership gains steam
articles.summary: Bernie Sanders and Elissa Slotkin say they will not support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader, calling for a new generation of leadership.
articles.body: Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., says he will not support Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., to serve as Senate majority leader once Democrats take control over the chamber next year. Sanders was complimentary of Schumer, but said at a news conference on Tuesday that he believes "the time is now" for change in Democratic leadership. "I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. [There’s] nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be re-elected as the Democratic leader," Sanders said at a news conference. CHUCK SCHUMER AFTER SWEEPING DEMOCRATIC MIDTERM VICTORIES: 'I'LL BE RE-ELECTED AS MAJORITY LEADER' Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., joined Sanders at the Tuesday news conference and said she also will not be supporting Schumer. Neither has backed a specific candidate to replace Schumer, however. "I am not actively seeking this job. I am seeking change," Slotkin said. "I’ve been very consistent for a very long time that we need a new generation of leadership … It’s important to demonstrate that we’ve heard what people want from this last election." THE HITCHHIKER’S GUIDE TO WHAT HAPPENS NEXT ON CAPITOL HILL Sanders and Slotkin join many Senate newcomers in opposing Schumer's re-election, including the likes of Sens.-elect Adam Hamilton and Troy Jackson. A number of the more left-wing Democrats favor Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for the new leader. SCHUMER DUCKS QUESTION ON CAMPAIGNING WITH SOCIALIST CANDIDATE WHO REFUSES TO BACK HIM AS LEADER "I’ve said very clearly that we need to have a discussion in the Democratic caucus," Van Hollen said during an appearance at Crooked Con over the weekend. "We need to understand what the Democrats are going to do with this new responsibility and these new powers," he continued. "And that nobody should get a blank check without a full understanding from the caucus as to where we’re going to go." articles.title: Trump targets New York Times over coverage of Bedminster suit, C-SPAN call
articles.summary: President Trump on Wednesday blasted The New York Times over its reporting on a sexual harassment settlement in connection with his Bedminster, N.J., golf club, as well as his recent phone call into C-SPAN. “The New York Times incorrectly reported that ‘Mr. Trump called into the premier of a C-Span show, APPARENTLY WITHOUT NOTICE.’ This…
articles.body:
President Trump on Wednesday blasted The New York Times over its reporting on a sexual harassment settlement in connection with his Bedminster, N.J., golf club, as well as his recent phone call into C-SPAN.

“The New York Times incorrectly reported that ‘Mr. Trump called into the premier of a C-Span show, APPARENTLY WITHOUT NOTICE.’ This is WRONG,” Trump wrote on Truth Social early Wednesday morning.

“It was a fully scheduled call, as a favor to C-Span, set up through White House Communications. It was done at C-Span’s request, not mine,” he added. “The Times knew this, but lied, in order to demean – But this is the least of their lies!”

Trump posted again less than a half hour later, writing that the “failing New York Times wrote about the ‘settling of a sexual harassment suit brought years ago by a waitress at President Trump’s golf club in Bedminster, N.J.'”

“What they fail to say is that it did not involve President Trump, a rather important omission,” Trump wrote. “FAKE NEWS!!!”

Both Times stories were published Tuesday. The outlet noted, as part of a larger story, that Trump’s call to “Washington Journal Primetime” was “unannounced” and “not on the president’s public schedule” before describing the on-air interaction.

Host Mimi Geerges asked Trump about his recent remarks suggesting that his deportation agenda hurt Republicans in the midterm elections. She tried to press Trump on this and other topics, with the president replying that the U.S. had not put sufficient pressure on countries releasing what “we call … the worst of the worst” from “mental institutions.”

The other Times story reported that the New Jersey Supreme Court’s Office of Attorney Ethics recommended that Alina Habba Mildon, New Jersey’s former top prosecutor, should face discipline for brokering a sexual harassment settlement involving a waitress at Trump’s golf club, claiming there were ethics violations.

This claim is in connection to interactions before Trump hired Mildon to be his personal lawyer. She had previously been a member of the golf club and befriended then-waitress Alice Bianco before later serving as her attorney.

The ethics complaint against Mildon, filed on Tuesday, could put her license to practice law at risk, The Washington Sun reported .

Alice Bianco sued the golf club in 2023, alleging that she was sexually harassed by her boss before signing a nondisclosure agreement, which New Jersey forbids in harassment cases. She later accepted a $15,000 settlement as part of “terms favorable to the golf club and unfavorable to Bianco,” the complaint states.

The complaint accuses Mildon of “divided loyalties” as a dues-paying member of the golf club.

Mildon’s attorney Kim D. Ringler told the Times that the complaint’s claims were “narrow” but that “we will work together to reach a fair and proportionate result, given the relatively less serious claims of professional misconduct from 2021.”

Mildon, the former acting U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey, stepped down from that role in December 2025 after a three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit affirmed a lower court’s ruling that she had not been lawfully serving since her interim term expired in July 2025.

articles.title: The end of the death penalty in California is a fresh start for justice
articles.summary: Now comes the work of building a justice system that earns the trust of every survivor and community it serves.
articles.body:
California has not executed anyone in 20 years . With his decision to commute the sentences of the 548 people on death row, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) has taken a historic step toward ending the death penalty in our state. Just as important, he has given California an opportunity to build something better in its place.

As the elected district attorney for Santa Clara County, I have not always been opposed to capital punishment. In fact, I sought death sentences in multiple cases. But over the years, I have grown convinced that our death penalty system simply cannot guarantee fairness to all.

In particular, visiting the Equal Justice Initiative’s Legacy Museum in Montgomery, Alabama opened my eyes to the inextricable link between racial terror lynchings and modern-day executions. As I stood at the memorial honoring thousands who were killed in lynchings — and contemplated the law enforcement officials who condoned and even participated in these killings — I asked myself whether there is any such thing as a moral execution.

In 2020, I stopped seeking capital punishment altogether. In 2024, I asked the courts to resentence 12 men my county had sent to death row. I had no reason to doubt their guilt, but every exonerated person was once someone a prosecutor was sure about. Only hubris would deny that it could happen in my office, too.

We have seen it happen too many times. Nationally, more than 200 people sentenced to death have been exonerated since 1973. Eight of them were in California, and all eight were men of color. It is why, in 2002, Santa Clara County became the first in the country to establish a Conviction Integrity Unit to ensure we could remedy mistakes made in the past.

Over my years as a prosecutor, I’ve also come to recognize that the death penalty’s failures reach the families of murder victims, who deserve far more from our justice system.

Never will I minimize the pain of losing someone to murder. Every murder destroys an entire universe of possibilities, for the person killed and for everyone who loved them. I have also learned that survivors are not a monolith. Some want the ultimate punishment. Many want something else: answers, safety, acknowledgment and the chance to stop reliving the worst day of their lives in a courtroom.

For those families, California’s death penalty has been a promise it could never keep. A death sentence here does not bring finality. It brings decades of appeals, new hearings and fresh headlines, each one reopening the wound. In Santa Clara County, two men sentenced to death in 1997 still did not have their direct appeals fully briefed more than 20 years later . Several others were still waiting for the state to assign them a lawyer. That is not justice delayed. It is justice suspended indefinitely, with victims’ families left waiting in the hallway.

The numbers tell the same story. California has spent more than $6 billion on capital punishment since 1978 and carried out 13 executions. Of the California death sentences that have completed judicial review, more than eight in 10 have been reversed. If any other unit in a prosecutor’s office had that failure rate, we would slam on the brakes and demand change.

And the burden has never fallen evenly. Black Californians are about 6 percent of the state’s population but more than one-third of its death row. And defendants of any race are up to 8.8 times more likely to be sentenced to death when at least one victim is white. Some may decide that a crime is horrific enough that these inequities don’t matter, but I cannot.

Gov. Newsom’s commutations recognize these failures of the death penalty, but they do not erase a single conviction or open a single prison door. What they remove is one of the gravest fears any prosecutor carries: that the state might execute an innocent person. Ending death sentences is more than a recognition of what has gone wrong. It is an opportunity to build something better. Freed from endless capital litigation, California can put its resources where they actually make communities safer and help survivors heal.

I have seen it happen. After I stopped seeking capital punishment, my office significantly narrowed the scope of post-conviction litigation, freeing up time, money and staff that allowed us to provide swifter, more tangible justice to victims’ families.

Statewide, the same shift opens the door to real investment: violence prevention and mental health care for at-risk youth, rehabilitation programs that make prisons safer, better law enforcement training and courts no longer clogged by decades-old cases. Most of all, it lets us invest in the resources crime victims and survivors need.

A prosecutor’s duty is not just to win cases, but to seek justice. That includes recognizing when the system itself is causing harm. Newsom saw that clearly and chose what is right over what is politically easy, showing that public safety, real accountability and respect for human dignity can go together.

Equal Justice Initiative founder and executive director Bryan Stevenson has long asked whether we deserve to kill. California has answered. Now comes the work of building a justice system that earns the trust of every survivor and community it serves.

Jeff Rosen has served since 2011 as the Santa Clara County district attorney.

articles.title: Video shows man tackled by ICE officers in front yard of California home
articles.summary: (KRON) – New doorbell video shows a man being tackled and arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in the front yard of a San Mateo, California, home. The incident happened shortly after 7 a.m. on Nov. 6. The San Mateo County Rapid Response Network said it has documented 21 ICE arrests over the…
articles.body:
( KRON ) – New doorbell video shows a man being tackled and arrested by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers in the front yard of a San Mateo, California, home.

The incident happened shortly after 7 a.m. on Nov. 6.

The San Mateo County Rapid Response Network said it has documented 21 ICE arrests over the past 10 days, including five on Tuesday alone. Officers were reportedly spotted at several locations, including Home Depot and Dollar Tree parking lots in San Carlos and Chavez Supermarket in Palo Alto.

The Rapid Response Network connects people detained by ICE with legal assistance and helps their families navigate what comes next.

But spokesperson Nani Friedman said the organization is now fundraising to keep those services available.

“Creating so much fear and concern in the community and having a big impact on the families,” Friedman said. “We know that those families are at risk of homelessness. We know that their children struggle to stay in school, to focus on their education, so it’s an important opportunity for our community to come together and provide them some support.”

San Mateo County Board of Supervisors President Noelia Corzo said the latest arrests are alarming and heartbreaking. She said the county has been preparing for an increase in federal immigration enforcement.

“You know, I understand the pain and the anger. I’m going to try and not get emotional myself,” Corzo said. “So if and when folks were detained, very quickly they would have access to attorney support for habeas actions to get them released. We’ve had our rapid response network up and running for 10 years.”

Friedman said one of the most important things people can do right now is make sure they know how to reach the network.

“It’s crucial to save your Rapid Response Network in your phone and spread the word,” Friedman said.

Nexstar’s KRON reached out to ICE for more information about the latest arrests. The agency provided a list of people arrested across California but did not specify where or when those arrests took place.

Meanwhile, Corzo is encouraging residents to attend Monday’s Board of Supervisors meeting.

Corzo plans to propose a cease-and-desist action, alleging ICE officers have been using county property to park or stage before making arrests. She said her goal is to protect the county’s existing noncollaboration ordinance.

articles.title: Hegseth could face new impeachment push over Ukraine aid, lawmakers warn
articles.summary: War Secretary Pete Hegseth could face new articles of impeachment over Ukraine military aid as House Democrats prepare to take control of Congress.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Some House Democrats are leaving the door open to additional articles of impeachment against War Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of military aid to Ukraine, according to lawmakers who spoke with Fox News Digital after a failed impeachment effort led by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie. But a conservative legal expert suggested the renewed impeachment push may be less about removing Hegseth from office than discouraging conservatives from serving in future Republican administrations. Massie, R-Ky., told Fox News Digital that while he could not substantiate allegations that Hegseth improperly withheld military assistance to Ukraine, he believes Democrats will investigate the matter and potentially introduce additional articles of impeachment when they take control of Congress in January. "I believe [Democrats] may use some of the same articles of impeachment when they're in the majority, but I also believe there are gonna be some other articles of impeachment based on hearings and committees," Massie told Fox News Digital. "I think the Democrats will do that." DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY "I heard that as one of the complaints that wasn't in my impeachment resolution," Massie added. Massie acknowledged that another impeachment effort could be largely symbolic if the Senate fails to convict Hegseth, but argued that the proceedings could still pressure the war secretary to resign. While impeachment requires a simple majority in the House, conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority in the Senate. Massie said he hopes a Democratic-controlled Senate would hold a trial if the House impeaches Hegseth. "So there's still a reason to proceed," Massie said. His remarks came after the House rejected his effort Tuesday to impeach Hegseth over military operations against Iran and suspected drug smugglers in the Atlantic and Pacific oceans without congressional authorization. The Constitution grants Congress the power to declare war, while the president, as commander in chief, has authority to direct military operations. The extent to which a president can initiate hostilities without congressional authorization remains legally disputed. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., also called on the House Monday to impeach Hegseth and urged the Senate to hold a trial to remove him from office. Schumer did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Zach Smith, a legal fellow at the Heritage Foundation, criticized Democrats' plans to pursue impeachment and potential prosecution of Trump administration officials, calling the efforts an "unfortunate waste of time" given the two-thirds Senate majority required to convict and remove an impeached official. Smith argued, however, that Democrats are prioritizing impeachment proceedings to discourage conservatives from serving in future Republican administrations, not to actually remove Hegseth. He added that the efforts would also divert congressional attention from "the many very important issues that our country is facing today," including concerns Democrats campaigned on ahead of the midterm elections, such as driving down the cost of living. "Not only does this mean that the House and the Senate will have to take time away from the legislative activities they should be focusing on, but it will also make it more difficult for members of the Trump administration to do their duties as well, because they'll have to be dealing with these requests and other efforts by Congress," Smith told Fox News Digital. Despite Smith's concerns, Rep. Adelita Grijalva, D-Ariz., echoed Massie's expectations, telling Fox News Digital that she anticipates congressional oversight committees will investigate Hegseth's handling of military assistance to Ukraine. Grijalva said she expects congressional committees to hold hearings examining Hegseth's handling of Ukraine funding. ‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH "This is an issue that will come up again, because once we have more information into how bad his handling has been, we will likely have more movement and possibly more articles of impeachment," Grijalva told Fox News Digital. The Arizona Democrat, who described herself as "a big believer in process and getting the facts out," argued that voters sent a clear message during the 2026 midterm elections. Grijalva said Americans spoke "very clearly" when they voted, signaling that "they want to put an end to the corruption." Fox News Digital could not independently verify the allegation that Hegseth improperly withheld Ukraine funding or engaged in any wrongdoing related to the matter. Hegseth did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., told Fox News Digital that he had "no idea" whether additional impeachment articles would be introduced and was unaware of evidence supporting the allegations. However, he expressed support for removing Hegseth from office. "I will fully support impeaching him," Wiener told Fox News Digital. "He's a disaster to our military and our country." Republicans, meanwhile, accused Democrats of pursuing politically motivated impeachment proceedings against Trump administration officials. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital following Tuesday's vote that he was "not surprised" by Democrats' interest in impeaching Hegseth. Mast argued that Democrats were determined to impeach "anyone who was appointed by the president," regardless of whether evidence supported the allegations. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The discussions come as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, giving the party greater power to launch investigations, hold hearings and pursue impeachment proceedings.

articles.title: Mulvaney: ‘Animosity aimed at the White House right now is real’
articles.summary: Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney suggested that President Trump’s grip on congressional Republicans is weakening amid growing frustration with the White House following the GOP’s midterm losses. “The animosity aimed at the White House right now is real,” Mulvaney said during an appearance on NewsNation, adding that he has spoken with some…
articles.body:
Former White House chief of staff Mick Mulvaney suggested that President Trump’s grip on congressional Republicans is weakening amid growing frustration with the White House following the GOP’s midterm losses .

“The animosity aimed at the White House right now is real,” Mulvaney said during an appearance on NewsNation, adding that he has spoken with some senators in recent days.

“I don’t think the Republicans on the Hill are taking their marching orders from Donald Trump nearly the same as they were two weeks ago. The Senate is going to do what they want to do,” he added.

Mulvaney’s remarks come after the Democrats secured a stunning victory in the elections last week. The party is set to take control of both the House and Senate after notching big wins in battleground states like Texas, Michigan, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and South Carolina.

While the GOP suffered upsets across the board, they continued to maintain a strong hold in states like Florida. By current tally, the Democrats will hold 54 Senate seats come January, with two seats yet to be called , and a House majority, according to Decision Desk HQ.

The “ blue wave ” was promptly followed by calls for the impeachment of top officials in the administration, with a spotlight on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The efforts against Hegseth were spearheaded by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) who introduced eight articles of impeachment — accusing the defense secretary of abusing his powers with regards to several miliary operations throughout the second Trump administration, including the war in Iran.

“I have Hegseth on my top three scalps that Democrats want to claim sometime in the next Congress,” Mulvaney said Tuesday.

Earlier in the day, House Republicans voted to shelf the impeachment measure in a tight 211-204 vote, essentially placing a halt on the effort until the next Congress when Democrats will be in power.

“It’s good news that he dodged the bullet here, but face it, after January 3rd, the numbers in that chamber are going to be dramatically different,” the former White House aide added.

articles.title: Republicans are ‘going to have to start moving on’ from Trump: Erick Erickson
articles.summary: Conservative commentator Erick Erickson decried President Trump’s postelection messaging, criticizing the president for doubling down on remarks that the midterms were “rigged” after his party’s big losses. “The Republicans are going to get pummeled in 2028 if they don’t figure this out,” Erickson told NewsNation’s Lauren Wright. “The message to Republicans needs to be, ‘Get…
articles.body:
Conservative commentator Erick Erickson decried President Trump’s postelection messaging, criticizing the president for doubling down on remarks that the midterms were “rigged” after his party’s big losses.

“The Republicans are going to get pummeled in 2028 if they don’t figure this out,” Erickson told NewsNation’s Lauren Wright. “The message to Republicans needs to be, ‘Get over your denial. You got your butt kicked because of tariffs, the war, prices, immigration and also corruption.'”

After Republicans’ sweeping losses in last week’s midterms, Trump initially said he accepted the results of the election. But in the days since, he has made baseless accusations of election fraud multiple times on Truth Social.

“Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” Trump wrote Monday. “It’s all about the machines.”

Erickson said he was surprised Trump doubled down on claims of election fraud and other unpopular positions that may have cost Republicans in the midterms, saying other presidents have usually pivoted away from the positions that cost their party.

“The bigger shock really is that the president and the White House have decided to double down as opposed to pivoting after the election,” Erickson said. “Clinton, Bush, Obama and even Biden, to a degree, all pivoted after midterms. Trump’s going to double down.”

Trump’s unpopularity, partly driven by inflation, tariffs and the fallout from the Iran war, contributed to a brutal midterm election for the GOP. Democrats won Senate seats in places where they have not won in decades , including South Carolina , Kansas, Texas and possibly even Mississippi , though no winner has been projected in the close Senate race there.

The losses initially contributed to some Republicans pushing back on the Trump agenda, including Vice President Vance, who made clear he thought the Iran war was why the GOP did so poorly.

But if serious pushback looked likely, Republicans quickly unified against Democrats. The party banded together to stop a Republican-led effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth Tuesday, chose Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) — a conservative member of the caucus — to serve as House minority leader , and shut down a challenge to their Senate leader, Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.).

And after briefly signaling openness to work with Democrats on some issues, namely immigration reform, Trump sent a different signal by naming immigration hard-liner Stephen Miller as his White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Erickson cautioned Republicans against standing firm behind the president, saying it may be in their best interest politically to distance themselves.

“This is Donald Trump being Donald Trump, and the party needs to realize that he’s now a lame duck and they’re going to have to start moving on from him,” he added.

articles.title: John Thune re-elected as US Senate Republican leader after midterm losses
articles.summary: The Republican ran unopposed, despite some GOP lawmaker demands to evaluate the party’s stinging midterm losses to Democ
articles.body:
As they prepare to lose power, Republicans in the United States Senate have re-elected John Thune to lead their party during the final years of Donald Trump’s presidency.

At a closed-door meeting at the US Capitol on Tuesday, the South Dakota lawmaker won the support of his fellow Senate Republicans – even as some had hoped to delay the leadership vote to examine what went wrong in last week’s election.

“I appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today”, Thune said in a statement after the vote. “I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress.”

Unlike two years ago, when he competed against two of his fellow Republicans to replace outgoing Senator Mitch McConnell as the party’s Senate leader, Thune ran unopposed on Tuesday for the role.

Senator Josh Hawley told reporters after the vote that “maybe there would be” a challenger if Senate Republicans had waited longer.

“I just think that we’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?” the Missouri Republican said.

Republican Senator Ron Johnson, who circulated a letter asking for a delay in the vote, said he tried to postpone the leadership decision. He said his conference needed to do some “real soul searching” but, like Hawley, conceded that no one else had stepped up to challenge Thune.

“That’s part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said as he turned to a reporter and joked, “Do you want it?”

Thune’s re-election comes as Republicans in the US House selected Speaker Mike Johnson’s successor. Congressman Jim Jordan was elected as the US House minority leader, marking his first foray into Republican leadership.

Under Thune’s tenure, US Republicans lost at least seven Senate seats in the country’s pivotal midterms . Two US Senate races – Alaska and Mississippi – still remain uncalled.

Despite those losses, some in the party, like Senator Jim Lankford of Oklahoma, said that there is “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has taken a markedly different approach than McConnell to seek out differing viewpoints before making major decisions.

“It’s a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said of Thune’s role. “No one wants that job”.

Some conservative voices have attributed the party’s losses to Thune’s effort to pass the SAVE America Act, which would have required proof of US citizenship for voters and mandated voters to present identification when casting their ballot.

But on Tuesday, after winning re-election, he said backlash from voters was bigger than just one piece of legislation.

“Well, I think in every election, it’s never any one thing”, Thune told reporters. “I think it was a combination of things and, most importantly, it was the cost of living for the American people”.

The Republican leader had previously tried to raise the alarm on affordability, including rising global energy prices, in the lead-up to the midterms. During a Fox News interview in September, Thune said Trump’s war in Iran , which he once said would not be a “long-term thing”, had “trumped everything else” for US voters.

He has also emphasised Israel’s right to self-defence and criticised policies that pressure the Israeli military’s operations.

“Both the president and the Democrat leader are entitled to their personal strategic opinions and their personal opinions on Israel’s leadership,” Thune said in response to remarks by former President Joe Biden and then-Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer in 2024. “What they are not entitled to is to attempt to dictate the election process or the strategic planning of a sovereign nation.”

Over the next two years, Thune will have to contend with a White House that has indicated it wants to double down on its most controversial policies while working to prevent further Republican losses in the 2028 election. He will also have to work with a Democratic-controlled Congress if Republicans hope to advance any legislation.

Thune, however, said he is looking forward to the “important work” that lies ahead.

“I’m proud of what this Republican team has accomplished together,” he said. “We remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats’ efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda”.
